subsubtopic: IMPACT ON CANADIAN CONSUMER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon, Canadians had their hour of truth.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought down a budget for the rich and for the multinationals. The rich received a present of $125,000 cash in the form of a capital gains exemption, and if their accountants have any imagination, they will not pay a cent of surtax for 1985-86.
A few months ago, the Conservative Government proposed to do away with the off-oil subsidy for switching from oil to other forms of energy such as gas or electricity.
Government Members told us that these drastic cutbacks, which affected the average Canadian, were necessary to reduce the deficit. A few weeks later, they signed an agreement with the multinational oil companies, giving away $2 billion in the process.
Yesterday afternoon, the Minister of Finance confirmed what we said when the agreement was signed: that Canadians would pay for this. The 2 cents per litre increase in the price of gas, which will probably cost the Canadian consumer about 4 cents a litre, is a measure that is anti-Canadian and pro-multinationals.
The Conservatives showed their true colours yesterday afternoon, and this Government ought to be ashamed of the way it is selling Canadians out to the multinationals.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS PROPOSED CUTS IN EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS
FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS PROPOSED CUTS IN EQUALIZATION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night's Budget continued the previous Liberal Government's attack on transfer payments provided to the provinces. It is ironic that the House, which is presently debating legislation reinstating
some of the money to our have-not provinces, including Quebec, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island, and Nova Scotia, lost as a result of Liberal Government cut-backs, now learns that the Conservatives intend to cut further transfer payments due under the existing formula by $2 billion.
That money is earmarked for post-secondary education and medicare in all provinces, and for equalization payments in our less rich areas. Equalization payments are guaranteed in our Constitution in recognition of the importance of maintaining a certain level of essential services to all Canadians regardless of where they live in Canada.
To attack these payments, in addition to funds for health care and post-secondary education, proves that the Government cares little for the plight of ordinary Canadians. The Government claims that it is a tough but fair Budget. It is tough to those who need assistance, and very fair, indeed generous, to those who need to be taxed more in order to pay their share of the legitimate costs of government.

subsubtopic: SUPPORT FOR FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has not been the only one who has undertaken an extensive pre-budget consultation process. Like all government Members, I have been involved in an extensive program of consultation with many business, social, and other groups in my riding. I try to meet with as many of my constituents as possible at every opportunity. I can say that during the last few months I have met with a very large number of constituents, and I would like to share with the House the results of my comprehensive consultation process.
In my riding I found overwhelming support for fiscal responsibility and a realistic Budget or, as the Minister of Finance and the rest of my constituents have called it, a tough Budget. However, there was an equally strong feeling that the Budget must also be fair-fair and equitable. They told me that we, as a Government, could not and should not lose sight of those people who truly required our assistance. I think all will agree that we did not lose sight of them. We have asked all Canadians to share the responsibility for the deficit, and we have also asked those who can, to assist us in dealing with it. I am confident that it is the sense of equity and fairness which will ensure that this tough Budget receives the overwhelming support of all Canadians.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET ON FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the only farmers to receive relief in yesterday's Budget were those who have given up and are quitting. Otherwise, agriculture, an industry in crisis, was singled out for particularly severe impact. Consultation with farmers failed. Fifty million dollars per year in grants and contributions are being removed. The cost recovery program of $33 million is still in place, and is being added to by a cost recovery program for the Grain Commission. Cuts in transportation subsidies are being increased. There is no mortgage relief, no agri-bonds, no Section 31 relief for part-time farmers. Research is a low priority. Crop insurance assistance is being cut back. There is an increase of two cents per litre in energy cost which is not rebatable. There is a general increase of 1 per cent in excise tax on all farm inputs.
Rural Canada, which sent many Members to form the Conservative majority, has been betrayed again. Farmers out there planting today know that they are being squeezed once more by the Government.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the main concern of Canadians is jobs, and yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated that the Budget's priority goal is jobs for Canadians.
In order to stimulate the investment needed to create those jobs, the Budget proposes a lifetime capital gains tax exemption of half a million dollars for every Canadian, measures to encourage greater investment in small business by pension funds, and a 100 per cent annual tax credit refund for qualifying research and development on the first $2 million of expenditures.
These measures, together with the Western Energy Accord, are aimed at promoting economic growth and creating jobs in the three areas of the economy most likely to result in the greatest and fastest response, small business, research and development, and the petroleum industry. The capital gains exemption, for example, should give small business a boost to expand. There are over 700,000 small businesses in Canada. The Canada Assistance Plan (CAP) enables federal sharing in the costs to provinces and municipalities of providing a wide range of assistance benefits to needy victims of family violence. These benefits include social assistance allowances, subsidized legal services, assistance with the cost of non-insured medical expenses, maintenance of the family in a transitional home or other sheltered environment. The families may also benefit from services such as day care for children, home support, crisis intervention and counselling, employment support and information/referral services.
As mentioned, one of the forms of assistance to needy victims of family violence is the maintenance of the family in a sheltered environment. These sheltered environments may be

In 1983-84 cost sharing was effected on behalf of needy women and their children in 63 transition and crisis centres in the country. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we end the hockey season and enter the baseball season, I would like to remind the House, particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), of his famous namesake who played for the Giants and the Chicago Cubs, Hack Wilson. On reading the history of the National League, I see that Hack probably received more razzing than any other player in the circuit, particularly when he struck out, which was often. The Minister of Finance struck out yesterday. We say to him very sincerely that we are disappointed that he did.

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
We Liberals have a view of budgets which I would like to deal with briefly. We believe that budgets are to serve people. They are to provide Canadian people with working opportunities, an equitable and a fair tax system and, to draw upon the words of the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we as Liberals must strive to raise ever higher the standard of life and of living of Canadians. That is what budgets are designed to do, or should be designed to do. Laurier was not speaking of just some Canadians. He was speaking of all Canadians in all regions of this great country, in all sectors-agriculture, fisheries, forestry, mines, plant workers et cetera.

Mr. Speaker, we in the Liberal Party believe the Budget should serve all Canadians and not just one group of Canadians.

We see the strength and the growth of the economy as imperative, not for the economy's sake, but for the people's sake. The economy is there to serve the people of Canada. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to other Members of this House that this Budget handed down by our Minister of Finance establishes a clear line of demarcation between Conservative ideology on the one hand and Liberal principles on the other.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Liberals have believed, continue and always will believe that the private sector is the engine of growth in this country. The Tories say they do too. What is the difference? Liberals define the private sector as comprising all Canadians: children, youth, consumers, the unemployed, working men and women, the elderly, the retired, business and labour. For Liberals, all Canadians constitute the private sector. The Tories define the private sector as comprising only the business community and those who can afford to invest. We as Liberals say that the kind of growth that this country requires, the jobs that we require need the participation of all Canadians, not just the business community and those who can afford to invest. All must participate in this growth and all must benefit from it.
That is not the case with this Budget. Here we have a first class example of the celebrated trickle-down theory. John Kenneth Galbraith, as you know, refers to this approach as horse and sparrow economics. You feed the horse enough and you hope and pray that something will be left over for the sparrows. Even worse, in this Budget there is such a heavy tax burden on Canadian consumers that demand will be dampened, unemployment will increase and, moreover, inflation will increase. The Minister of Finance knows that. In fact, he said that. Of course, the deficit is likely to increase as well.
Liberals believe in managing the public debt, controlling spending, but using the engine of growth with the co-operation of all consumers and investors, first, to control and then, of course, to reduce the deficit, a deficit I might say, notwithstanding all the declarations of those opposite, which was not
brought about by profligate spending by the previous Government. There has been some profligate spending, I might add, since the Tories have taken office. It was a deficit incurred, as Canadians know and appreciate, to cushion Canada and Canadians against the ravages of the worst recession since the 1930s.
Let me translate those thoughts on growth, from the Liberal point of view, into numbers. The last Liberal Budget, as the documents deposited by the Minister of Finance clearly show, indicate a real growth rate last year as a result of the Liberal Budget of 4.7 per cent. That is for 1984. The Minister of Finance tells us that this year the Tories anticipate a growth rate of 3.1 per cent. He tells us more, that next year he anticipates a growth rate of 2.4 per cent. That is in 1986. Similarly, under the last Liberal Budget, personal income increased in 1984 by 7 per cent. The Tories expect this to decline in the current year to 6.8 per cent and next year to see it decline further to 5.9 per cent. Canadians will soon remind themselves once again that Tory times are tough times.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I predict that they will be kicking themselves for having forgotten that lesson in September of 1984. The Minister tells us about the climate of confidence that he wishes to create. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I ask the Minister of Finance, how can Canada have confidence when this Government has systematically broken promise after promise? Confidence will only be built upon credibility. This Government has lost its credibility. Those promises will be reviewed by speakers of this Party during the budget debate as we deal with the various sectors which are affected adversely by the proposals of the Minister of Finance.
One of the most recent commitments of the Minister of Finance was made as recently as on March 1 when he appeared on the program Question Period. In response to questions from Mr. Terrence Wills of the Montreal Gazette, he said:
I don't want to increase taxes, Terry. I think we have a good deal of scope on the expenditure side to deal with the deficit problem. A tax increase, certainly a general tax increase, puts a dampening effect on the economy and I don't want to see us do that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who said that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance said that. Not only was that a breach of a commitment that we witnessed yesterday and not only does it affect the credibility of the Minister, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government, but it carries very serious consequences in terms of job loss, not job creation in this country, and that is strike one against the Minister.
Recently, Pierre Lortie, the President of the Montreal Stock Exchange, with whom I am sure the Minister consulted at some length, made some comments with respect to raising taxes in a speech he gave early this month in Toronto. At that time, he said:
May 24, 1985

The problem with raising taxes lies with their indirect effects which are powerful. Raising taxes cools the economy in two ways. The first familiar effect is that taxes dampen demand. With 11 per cent unemployment, a 4 per cent inflation rate and a growth rate well below that of the U.S. economy, the Canadian economy surely does not need a cold shower.
He went on to say:
Thus, a strategy to reduce the deficit which would embody tax increases could be really hurtful to the Canadian economy.
It is pretty clear that any consultations the Minister may have had with Mr. Lortie were not heeded.
[ Translation]
-I personally would have gone further than Mr. Lortie. These tax increases will not only harm the economy, Mr. Speaker, but also and especially those Canadians who cannot protect themselves.

How many jobs will be lost? The Minister of Finance knows but he will not tell us. He will say, of course, as I have heard him say repeatedly on the radio, on television and here in the House, that it is the confidence factor which will not only replace those jobs which might be lost through some economic model study but will also create new jobs. I say to the Minister of Finance that there can be no confidence when there are these flagrant breaches of promises which have been made by the Minister and the Government. The Minister said that he did not want a general increase in taxes. We have witnessed a massive increase in taxes.
I know my colleagues have always believed in the integrity of the Minister of Finance. We can only come to the conclusion that once again he has lost a battle in Cabinet, once again he has been derailed. He did not want massive tax increases. He declared that his aim was not to have tax increases. Look at the increases that have been imposed upon us.
1 invite you, Mr. Speaker, to look at page 19 of The Fiscal Plan which tells us about new tax measures with major impacts on budgetary revenue. These numbers have been carefully caressed by netting some with others which should not be there. I am quite happy to explain my analysis of these numbers, but the bottom line of it is that in 1985-86, individual Canadians will be subjected to tax increases of $1,170 million, not the paltry $250 million which is shown at the bottom of that table, and in 1986-87, they will be subjected to tax increases of $4,360 million. I would be quite happy and anxious to debate my analysis of those numbers with the Minister of Finance.
I would point out that, among other things, I have eliminated in my calculations the so-called capital gains reduction from those revenues. Let me point out that we are talking about general tax increases. In 1982, the last year for which I have numbers, 63 per cent of all capital gains came from 4 per cent of Canadian taxpayers. I submit to the Minister of Finance that it is hardly fair game to net the lost revenue on the capital gains tax exemption against the tax increases which are going to be borne by ordinary Canadians from coast to coast. That, Mr. Speaker, is strike two. The Minister lost his battle in Cabinet. He had to submit to increased taxes, some-
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
thing which he knew was not the way to go in terms of deficit reduction.
The Minister promised us a fair Budget. Let us examine that proposition very briefly. How do these tax increases affect individual Canadians?

You know, people are going to remember the Progressive Conservative Government for its decision to promote capital gains to tax kids' candy, soap and pet food. This is of course a caricature, but the fact is that the combination of taxes introduced yesterday will crush the middle class and the poor, and I would like to give you a few examples.
For a married couple and I shall quote figures from the papers tabled in the House yesterday by the Minister for a married couple with only one income and two dependent children below the age of 18, and earning $20,000, taxes will go up $175, and that does not include sales tax, excise tax on tobacco or the tax on fuel. Altogether, it will mean an increase of at least $200 and probably more. Some people have estimated that the additional burden will amount to between $500 and $1,000 per family.

Of course, the Government and the Minister will argue and have already argued that the rich are also hit hard by this Budget. That is because of the temporary surtax which has been imposed upon them. Let us look at the circumstances of that same couple with one source of income and two dependent children. We see that carrying the tax provisions forward for the year 1990, the time frame within which the Minister of Finance spoke, the tax burden of that family at the $20,000 level will be increased by 17 per cent, using any reasonable assumptions such as those which were set forth in the table of the Minister himself. If, on the other hand, we look at a family at the $200,000 level, a family which could certainly be classified as being rich, we find that the increase will in fact be 2 per cent in the year 1990.
Many people seem to have lost sight of the fact that the surtax is an 18-month tax. It is only a blip, but the other provisions go on forever and penalize the low-income groups. In fact, if one uses that same 1982 capital gains tax distribution to which I referred a moment ago, we find that the taxpayer at the $200,000 level will pay $2,352 less in taxes in 1990. The 2 per cent figure I mentioned is there without reference to the capital gains tax break.
What about old age security? Simple calculations show that by the year 1990, the average old age security payment will be reduced by $30 per month or $369 per year. As I entered the House, I heard the Minister answering a question by saying that GIS had been indexed. However, G1S recipients, as we know, receive old age security and GIS. If the old age security costs them $30 per month, that effectively means that people who receive GIS will lose $30 per month. When the Liberal Government introduced its six and five program to cap indexation, that was taken into account. Accordingly, a double

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
indexation on GIS was provided for. The Minister has failed to do that. Elderly people at the poverty line will lose $30 per month in real dollars in the year 1990.
What about child benefits? We have calculated that once one reaches over $12,000 of income, everyone loses, and by 1990, something between $300 million and $380 million will have been taken out of the child benefit system. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this Budget is not only unfair, it is grossly unfair. That is strike number three for the Minister of Finance.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I was talking about people who have been adversely affected by this veritable avalanche of taxes. However, we must not forget the poorest regions of this country which have now been abandoned by the Progressive Conservatives, and especially the Atlantic Provinces and the Gaspe, for instance. In the course of this debate, you will be hearing a number of our Members who will elaborate on these questions. It is not only unfair to individuals but also unfair to the regions, and especially to the individuals living in those regions.

There is something else, Mr. Speaker, which I would like to bring to your attention, and 1 hope that you will take the opportunity to review the budget documents in detail. I reviewed them as best as I could in the time since yesterday, but I have much more to digest. It is apparent that the Budget is replete with what I call political arithmetic. What kind of climate of confidence can we expect to achieve in Canada if the Government is not forthcoming, does not give us the facts and does not tell us what will be the impacts of the various measures which have been introduced? It is one thing to tell us what the impact might be, but it is quite another to prepare the documents in such a manner that the presentation is confused and difficult to understand.
For example, there is the magic savings which the Conservative Government will accomplish by its New Management Initiatives. In 1985-86 alone, the magic savings will amount to $1.2 billion. The Conservatives call part of that plan "Improved Cash Management". Most of the better cash management will mean stripping and raping the Crown corporations of cash in the form of dividends. That is better cash management! A total of $366 million of the $1.2 billion will be saved in 1985-86. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will provide $26 million, Teleglobe Canada will provide $108 million; Petro-Canada will provide $50 million; Atomic Energy of Canada will provide $50 million, and Ports Canada will provide $83 million. I will not take the time of the House to read all of the corporations which will be involved in that savings plan as the documents are available for all to see. That is better cash management! Declaring dividends from Crown corporations has now become better cash management.
There is a point which I find most troubling and I hope at some point the Minister will furnish us with adequate explanations. After the brilliant exercise of saving $1.2 billion for better management practices, we find that the expenditures for 1985-86, as presented in the budget papers, will be $105 billion. When I turned to the Estimates which were tabled in the House several months ago, I found that expenditures in 1985-86 were to be $105 billion. How on earth can we explain what is going on? How can the Government maintain any credibility when it presents us with that kind of data?
In addition, there are no five-year projections in the Budget. I remember when his colleague, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), came into the House in 1979 and proudly proclaimed that he would introduce five-year projections. Of course, the reason he did so was that it was one of the most firm recommendations of the Lambert Commission on Financial Management and Accountability. He was the first Minister of Finance who had the opportunity to introduce those recommendations, and he did. He explained, at every occasion, the importance of having five-year projections. He explained the importance of allowing the public and others to scrutinize where the Government was intending to go. The Liberal Government which succeeded the Conservative Government of 1979 maintained that tradition through all the Budgets which were presented in the House. However, it has been abandoned by the Minister of Finance because he does not want to be forthcoming with Canadians. He does not want to tell the Canadian public where he is going to go.

What does he tell us? He tells us that between now and 1990, if I am not mistaken, he will reduce the deficit by $20 billion. But he does not want to give us forecasts, he does not want to show us how we will get there, he simply draws the conclusion.



-my constituency of Saint-Henri. Well, I would like to bring the Minister with me one of these days so he might explain to my constituents of Saint-Henri why they should pay taxes on candies and gasoline. But at the same time Ministers back here in Ottawa can increase their budgets, have well-paid staff and senior officials, not to mention the Prime Minister's Office. I really think he would have a hard time convincing the people of Saint-Henri in Montreal, which happens to be one of the regions hardest hit by this Budget.

Of course, we have seen the Government indulge in other exercises with taxpayers' money, while individual Canadians are having trouble making ends meet and living virtually from hand to mouth. But the Government treats itself to lavish spending and engages in bailing out corporations. I could cite the number of corporations which have been bailed out. They include Petromont, Domtar, the Canadian Commercial Bank, and Pioner Trust. At least those bail-outs were motivated by concerns of employment and investor confidence.
I hope the Minister of Finance takes these comments seriously because the example must be set here. This Government, of which he is a member, is the most lavish spender and the greatest squanderer of taxpayers' dollars on government lifestyle of all other Governments in the history of this country. It has the largest ministry with the largest staff. It has travelling committees to keep the back-benchers happy. Millions and millions of dollars are being squandered by the Government and by the Prime Minister with the circuses and showbiz to which we have been treated. As far as Quebec City is concerned, we have only seen the bill from CBC for $500,000. There was the Premiers' Conference and the Economic Summit. There has been no concern whatsoever for taxpayers' dollars. Yet the Minister of Finance had the gall to go on national television last night and say that Canadians would be pleased. He said that individual families who earn $20,000 or $30,000 a year would be pleased to pay an extra dollar a day in order to get the finances of the Government under control.
Where is the minimum tax when it comes to fairness? It is another lob hit by the Minister of Finance. He is a tennis player and he hits another lob on this one. That minimum tax would have gone a long way toward suggesting to ordinary men and women of this country that the Government means business, but there is no minimum tax. Instead, there is a study, further consultation, a series of options, and we are told the tax will be introduced miraculously in 1986. But no model for that tax has been decided upon. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you would join with me, if you could, and say that you will believe that tax when you see it.
In terms of expenditure, I must say that when we started to read about the expenditures of this Government on themselves, I really thought the sky was the limit. Now we learn, particularly when we watch the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), that not even the sky is the limit. In fact, all the skies
The Budget-Mr. Riis
of the world are open to the travelling Ministers of this Government.

It is unbelievable. When he was in Quebec City he was described as the "national air draft"-quite properly so. To him, that is just a few cents. He spent $57,000 to fly to Greece or wherever, and now the Minister of Finance is telling us that each Canadian family with an income of $20,000 to $30,000 ought to be proud to contribute $1 a day to control the finances of the federal Government. Unbelievable, Mr. Speaker, unbelievable!

We will be hearing much, Mr. Speaker, from Hon. Members on this side of the House with respect to the Budget and, believe me, there is much to be said. I want simply to conclude by telling the Minister of Finance, who unfortunately has left the House-and I should say in fairness to him that he told me he would have to leave the House at 12.40 p.m.-that there is one major difference between the Minister's namesake, Hack Wilson, and himself, that is that at least Hack Wilson hit a lot of home runs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to thank my colleagues in the House for the courtesy extended to me of an opportunity to speak perhaps a

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Riis
little bit beyond the 20-minute time limit, but certainly within the time limits followed by the previous speaker.
We have now waited as anxious parliamentarians for the last eight months, along with the people of Canada, for this budget presentation. It is the longest period of time in recent history that a Government has waited before it introduced a major Budget. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance prided themselves on having gone about the country and talked with groups in all regions, having spoken with organized groups such as the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and having listened to groups of individuals who were assembled at various conferences. But what has become very clear, Mr. Speaker, is that the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister seemed to have listened to a very select group when it came time to write out and introduce the Budget which we heard last night. I believe that when the dust settles over this whole matter, the columnists have had a chance to evaluate the situation and the true nature of the Budget is presented, what will become clear is that the boy from Baie Comeau has backed his Bay Street buddies all the way to the bank. Very clearly there was a bias in this particular Budget which went against the interests of ordinary Canadians and was very much in favour of a select group of Canadian society. That was perhaps reflected in the advice of the policy adviser brought in by the Minister of Finance for the Budget, the Vice-President of the Bank of Nova Scotia, who advised him on the approaches which the Minister ought to use and, indeed, this was a banker's Budget in many respects.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said that this was a tough Budget but a fair one. I suspect that the more appropriate wording would be that this was a very fair Budget for a very few number of Canadians and a very tough Budget for very many Canadians. What the privileged few in Canada received in this Budget was, of course, no introduction of the minimum tax which the Prime Minister promised Canadians would be introduced in this Budget. Those thousands of Canadians, whom we will call wealthy Canadians-the upper-income earners whose incomes are often in excess of $500,000-will again this year pay no income tax whatsoever as a result of the multitude of loopholes available to them in their financial arrangements.
There is another group of Canadians. We recognize that about 4 per cent of the Canadian population buy and sell stocks in the stock market, and a few more, perhaps, are interested in the matter of capital gains. The Government, through this Budget, has now introduced a capital gains holiday for those folks on the first $500,000 of income. That handful of Canadians who obtain their income from investments have now received a real bonus in this Budget and a lot of champagne will be consumed on the Bay Streets and in downtown Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver, as the senior executive levels celebrate just what this corporate giveaway means to them personally.
We think of the laid-off workers of the White Farm plant, the people who work at the heavy water plant in Cape Breton, the laid-off miners in the Highmont Mine in British Columbia
and the people who work at the Burns plant in Kitchener, and we wonder how excited they are today about the fact that they can escape capital gains tax on the first $500,000 of income earned through their investments.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are lucky if they earn that in their lifetime.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As my hon. leader indicates, they are lucky to earn that during their entire lifetime.
So let us recognize that for the privileged few this Budget is excellent news. There will be lots of champagne being drunk over the next few days as people celebrate this Budget.
On the other hand, for most Canadians, the average Canadian, what did the Budget have? Some extremely tough measures. When you examine the implications of the November 8 Economic Statement and add those to the provisions in this Budget, you find that the average family in Canada will be paying about $1,000 more in taxes. That means that $1,000 a family will be taken out of every single community across this country. In the Corner Brooks, the Moose Jaws, the Chicouti-mis and the Sudburys, thousands of communities across this country, $1,000 a family will be taken away and plunked down here in Ottawa for the federal Government. The Minister of Finance indicated there would be a fairness in this Budget. Is it fairness to ask every senior citizen in Canada receiving OAS to pay an extra $100 a year starting next year? This will add up to $255 million coming from the senior citizens of Canada to make up for the money the Government is going to lose in its capital gains giveaway. The seniors of this country are going to be paying for that capital gains holiday. The average Canadian family is going to be paying an extra $1,000 to make up for the give aways to the large oil companies.
To be very frank, Mr. Speaker, what this Budget means is that almost every single item in the average corner store in our communities will have a federal tax added to it. Kids' candy bars and pop, all the confectioneries in that store, shampoos and soap, the things families use every day, will all be taxed. Pet food will be taxed in an effort to raise money because somebody has to pay for these capital gains giveaways. I remember very distinctly that when the Western Accord was signed a few weeks ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) said that they made this deal to help the western provinces particularly, but that the taxpayers of Canada are not going to pay for it. There will be no increase in gasoline taxes as a result, she said. What happened in western Canada was that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources sat down for dinner with the provincial Premiers and the heads of the oil companies, and we as Canadian citizens are going to be asked to cough up hundreds of millions of dollars to pay the tab.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Expensive dinner.

Very expensive dinner, when you consider the 9 cents a gallon tax. What does that mean for people who travel
May 24, 1985

about the second largest country in the world? What does that mean for every product transported across this vast country? What does it mean for people who have to travel long distances to work, up into the forest, out into the mines, or commute long distances in metropolitan areas? This 9 cents a gallon tax will be felt right across this country, and at a time when we were hoping to see some disposable income invested at the local level to assist small business. But we are pulling hundreds of millions of dollars out of those communities and bringing them back here to Ottawa, and that will not help small business.
I think the most surprising thing in this Budget is that it totally ignored a group of Canadians. It failed to recognize the
1.475	million Canadians who are jobless today, including 500,000 young people. This is the International Year of Youth, a year when we should be paying special attention to young people. Surely in a country which is at all sensitive the Government should recognize that young people have a special role to play. At this time of year, on budget day, they are coming out of the colleges, universities, technical and vocational schools, and high schools, looking for summer employment or their first job, and what do they find in the Budget? I do not think the word "youth" was even mentioned in the Budget. The Minister spoke for an hour and a half and did not even mention the word; it is not part of his vocabulary. I do not think it is part of the Government's vocabulary. The words which are in the Government's vocabulary, of course, are words like "deficits"-
