-and "capital gains", "corporate confidence", but the word "youth" is not mentioned. Was there any reference at all to the 600,000 women who are jobless? There was virtually not a word in the Budget which would assist those
1.475	million people presently out of work, not a word to give them any hope or encouragement, to indicate that things are going to change in the weeks and months ahead.
The Government has said that we need to have faith because the small business sector will have a whole set of reasons to expand its operations and create jobs. Whether it is in Corner Brook, Glace Bay, Bathurst, Lac-Saint-Jean, Timmins, Moose Jaw, High River, Prince George or Kelowna, small businesses will be going out and expanding in the weeks and months ahead. But let us look at the Minister's constituency. Let us look at a business in Etobicoke. Let us look at that small corner store again. All of a sudden, as a result of this Budget, that store finds that all of the families who use the store are going to have $1,000 removed from their pockets. They will not have a thousand dollars next year to buy goods from that store. In addition, everything in that store has increased in
The Budget-Mr. Riis
price as a result of additional federal taxes. Is that corner store going to want to run out and expand its operation?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not likely.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This same scenario can be imagined across this country. When you take money out of every community in this country and reduce the purchasing power of Canadians, when you do not give any hope to those 1.5 million unemployed, including all those young people looking for work, are people going to go out and purchase goods and services? Are they going to go out and buy that new refrigerator, stove, car or set of clothes? No, they are not. The Government says it expects businesses to go out and expand their operations and hire new employees, but I think we are asking too much of the business community under these conditions. There has been no effort to create more demand for their products. There has been no effort to provide a reason for those businesses to go out and expand. Therefore, I really do not believe that the hope or expectation the Minister expressed today so many times will in fact be realized.
I am reminded of Peter Pan when I hear the Minister of Finance say time after time, "If we really believe, if we really believe, then we can fly. If we really believe businesses are going to create those jobs and they will run out and expand their operations, then they will". Well, surely we can have something better than a Tinker Bell approach to encouraging the business community of Canada to expand and create the necessary jobs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to look at some aspects of the Budget which were not mentioned. Sometimes it is more appropriate to look at the Budget and take note of what he failed to mention at all. One of the key sectors of our economy is tourism. Right across the country, whether it is in the provinces or the Territories, a lot of Canadians feel this is one area where there is a considerable amount of growth potential. But is there anything in the Budget to assist the tourist sector? Yes, there is something that will affect the tourist sector; the increase in gasoline prices will make it that much more expensive for American travellers to travel around Canada in their Winnebagos and so on, or Canadians for that matter. Also, we are going to increase liquor prices, and that will have a rather profound negative effect on the hospitality industry.
I notice it is one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I could continue a little later today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It being one o'clock, I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
At 1 p.m. the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Riis

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) had the floor. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget includes nearly six and a half pounds of paper. Yet there is nothing in this entire package for the unemployed in the country. There is not a single thing in the package for young people in Canada. We find it totally unacceptable that, with 70 per cent of our young people ouf of work today, there was not a single reference to them in the budget speech.
It is interesting to consider what is in the Budget. After looking at it very carefully it becomes perfectly clear that the Government believes that the most important resource in the country is the capital resource. The other day my friend, the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain), suggested that the most important resource is not the capital resource, but trees. We in this Party believe very strongly that the most important resources in the country are our human resources, our young people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is nothing in this six and a half pounds of budget material that is going to assist farmers in Canada. There is, however, something that will assist them to get out of the farming business. The capital gains exemptions will help them to get out of farming, but aside from that we find only agricultural cuts. The only assistance for the forest sector is that the federal tax on boom chains can now be deducted. The fisheries sector finds further cuts, the imposition of user fees, but no assistance. There is no assistance for the mining sector. Mr. Speaker, there is nothing in this Budget which will provide assistance to the hard-pressed resources sectors of the country.
I have already mentioned tourism. This was a wonderful gift for British Columbia. Mr. Bennett must be really happy as they are developing Expo '86 and attracting new tourists. Now the Government slaps on a gasoline tax and an additional liquor tax to make it more expensive for visitors to come into the country. That is not the way in which to encourage tourism. Yet that is the way in which the federal Government has assisted the province which is developing Expo '86.
Was there tax reform in the Budget? Was there an effort to impose that minimum tax on the rich as promised by the Prime Minister? There is no minimum tax in this Budget. The Government says it may study it and put it in the Budget next year. However, it did not stop to study the impact of imposing a tax of $1,000 on families. There was no hesitation in putting that in.
There was nothing done about the billions of dollars in corporate tax concessions used for mergers and takeovers that do not result in new jobs or product lines. There was no corporate tax expenditure included with the Budget to enable us to see the pros and cons of the various expenditure programs. There was no five year projection of the corporate taxes and what they mean for Canada as there is in American
Budgets. There was nothing in this Budget with regard to corporate or personal tax reform.
I am pleased to see that the Minister of Finance is now with us and listening to our speeches. He said that this is a new era and new approach. He said it is a chance to make over our country and refashion Canada. He said it is a new way of doing things.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He went on to say things like, "We mean to cut our costs and become more productive", and, "The private sector must be the main creator of jobs".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He said, "We look to the creative, innovative small business sector". He said, "This is a fiscally responsible Budget". He said that securing growth and jobs depends on our success in four basic areas; reducing and controlling inflation, increasing investment, reducing the Government's deficit, and improving our competitiveness.
Oh, I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, this was Marc Lalonde's Budget. I am sorry, I got the Budgets mixed up.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And the Tories clapped.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to thank my Conservative colleagues for their approval of those suggestions, but I was meaning to read from this Budget.
Is there a change or a new direction, Mr. Speaker? The Liberals increased taxes and gave more concessions to the corporations and we know what happened to the country. Nothing has changed from the Lalonde or MacEachen Budget. Nothing has changed. Only the actors have changed and the colour of the suits. The whole effort of the Government was to attack the deficit. This was the bogey-man that had to be slain. This was the dragon. Michael was out there with his sword hacking away at the deficit dragon. What was it that created the deficit, Mr. Speaker? It was the result of the Liberal monetary policy and mismanagement for years and years that resulted in a recession. The fact that it was costing us $1 billion a month in UIC alone was adding to the deficit. Something else has added to the deficit, the billions and billions of dollars in corporate loopholes for which we are getting very little, if anyting, in return. Those are billions of dollars and that is what created the deficit. The cast we were not collecting corporate tax, business tax, personal tax and sales tax because of the recession was another reason.
The New Democrats did their consulting as well. We did not talk with Bay Street and to stockbrokers. We spoke with main street and ordinary Canadians. We came up with something called "Canada Unlimited". We have 70 recommendations in this book on how to reduce the high levels of unemployment. That is what Canada Unlimited sets out to accomplish.
May 24, 1985

Time and time again what our proposals do is to set targets for inflation, to get inflation down. We set targets for research and development levels and we set targets for foreign aid. Why not set targets for unemployment to get unemployment down? Why not set that as a goal and implement strategies to accomplish it? Why not reform the tax system to provide more moneys for the communities of Canada to assist small businesses as opposed to having a tax policy that takes out a thousand dollars a household from every community in Canada and focuses it right back here in Ottawa? Why not give that money to the communities to develop proper job-creation and economic development schemes?
We propose a minimum tax in Canada Unlimited and a return to the pre-1982 tax rate days. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will remember the time when that legislation was introduced and we heard it said, "This is for all the upper income earners of the country. We are going to reduce the amount of tax that you have to pay". If we introduced that old tax rate and a minimum tax, we would raise $1.2 billion. If we did that, we could avoid de-indexing of the tax exemptions, the old age security, and the family allowance.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member knows better than that.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. Before the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) continues I must advise him, and I am sure he knows, that it is not permitted to make demonstrations of the kind he is making.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't be ridiculous. Of course it is.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we followed our proposal for tax reform in Canada Unlimited, we could eliminate the federal tax reduction and avoid the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings plan and we could avoid increases in taxes on children's candy, pop, pet food, and all of the confectionery found in our small corner stores. We could avoid taxes on almost everything we could find in the corner stores. We could avoid additional taxes on tobacco and liquor and we would still have $200 million left.
If we had introduced those two provisions only out of the 70 recommendations in Canada Unlimited we would save all of that unnecessary tax increase and still have $200 million which could be used on direct job creation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This was a Budget that asked Canadians to make a special sacrifice. It asked only certain Canadians to make a special sacrifice. Ordinary Canadians were asked to make an especially major sacrifice in the way of increased taxes and increased costs of transportation, which will be reflected in the cost of virtually every good transported across Canada. This Budget is especially punitive on the resource sectors of mining, fisheries, agriculture, tourism, and forestry.
Some people benefited, however. They are the ones who are in the upper income brackets. They are very happy as a result
The Budget-Mr. Riis
of this Budget because they can still use the loopholes of the tax system and pay not a single red cent of income tax. If that were not good enough, those people who obtain their income through investments and consequently take advantage of the capital gains provisions will get another holiday. They will not have to pay any tax at all on their capital gains until a half a million dollars has been accumulated. If we talk about the beneficiaries in this Budget, we are talking about a handful of Canadian citizens. The very wealthy in Canada will get much wealthier.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the farmers?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Hon. Member says, "What about the farmers?" We have six and a half pounds of budget papers. There is nothing for the farmers in this bundle other than to encourage them to get out of farming.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there anything in the budget papers to help young people get into farming and into food production? Is there any assistance for those farmers who are hard pressed financially in terms of a heavy debt equity ratio? Are there any agri-bonds in these papers to assist those hard-pressed farmers? No, there is nothing. Is there any clarification of Section 31 of the Income Tax Act? No, there is nothing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the small business bond?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is a small business bond. But show me a farmer who has been able to get a small business bond. Show me a single farmer who has been able to get one. That is the only bloody provision Mr. Speaker, to assist a farmer, but he cannot get one.
When you ask what is in the Budget for farmers, I say there is nothing, Sir. I can repeat those same comments for the fishermen, the miners, the loggers, the millworkers, and for the ordinary Canadians.
As a result, I am pleased to move on behalf of my Party, seconded by the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end of the last sentence to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words: "And this House further condemns the Government for actions which will effectively reduce pensions for senior citizens, for gasoline tax increases to pay for the Western Accord, for its failure to take immediate and determined action to reduce the ranks of the unemployed, and for the absence of a minimum tax on wealthy Canadians who pay no income tax."

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Having read the subamendment, I find it in order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a straightforward and sincere question for the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). In that we are both federal politicians and we both come from British Columbia, I would like the Hon. Member's comment on a question relating to forestry. We have arrived at an agreement with the Province of British Columbia, an agreement which was never reached before,

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Riis
regarding $300 million in reforestation and silviculture. It is part of the over-all commitment on the part of the Government to work in the forestry area. Does the Hon. Member not agree that this is a significant starting point in forestry, or is he completely against the program? He said that we have not done anything for forestry. In view of the fact that we made such a commitment and started such a productive program for forestry, does he concur with it, or is he totally against anything for forestry which we brought forward?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that normally the first speakers for each Party do not have an opportunity to respond to questions. I am pleased that the Speaker changed the rules for today to make this possible, and I welcome the questions of the Hon. Member.
He referred to the fact that I said that in the 6.5 pounds of budget material there was nothing for forestry-and I stand by that-with the exception of the removal of the federal tax on boom chains. There is nothing in the 6.5 pounds of budget material for the forestry industry.
The Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain) talked about the $300 million federal-provincial agreement to assist the forest sector. I remind him of the words of Les Reed, who used to be Deputy Minister of Forestry in Ottawa and is presently occupying the senior chair of forestry at the University of British Columbia, Department of Forestry. He made the observation that this $300 million was to be spent over five years and that to do the job necessary we needed $300 million this year and every year thereafter.
We should recognize that out of every dollar collected by the federal Government from the forest industry, it returns only five cents, a measly nickel. Yes, I suppose on the logn journey to the moon, one step is a step in the right direction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a couple of years ago the New Democratic Party had a task force to encourage involvement in the small business sector. I think that was laudable. Last night, Mr. John Bulloch, who represents that sector which the NDP wants to see flourish, said that the Budget would create a minimum of 400,000 jobs and maybe more. Yet the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) seems to imply that there is no job creation in the Budget. At the end of his speech he spoke about direct job creation. Would he define how he uses the term "direct job creation"? Does he agree with Mr. John Bulloch that the Budget could create a minimum of 400,000 jobs or more?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I recall from the budget documents-and I believe it was in The fiscal Plan-the term outlines the projected levels of unemployment in Canada. By his own admission, the figures of the Minister of Finance indicate that they will be in excess of 10 per cent for the rest of this decade. Beyond that it is anyone's guess. In dealing with unemployment, the Budget indicates that we will not deal with unemployment and that we will be doing other things because the Government's projection is that it will stay about the same.
I also remember what the two previous Ministers of Finance
projected unemployment to be, and of course the figure was much higher. When one starts to project into the future and depends totally on the whims of the market-place, it is made very difficult. By the Minister's own admission unemployment will not be improved.
When I heard John Bulloch the other day, I suspected that John was drinking a lot of his own bath water. I do not think John has visited many parts of Canada. I know the Prime Minister has not visited British Columbia since assuming office. If the Prime Minister had visited British Columbia, the Hon. Member's constituency and mine, he would know that we cannot stand idly by now and wish that jobs will be created and that small business will expand. That may apply to some parts of central Canada, but in the eartern, northern and western parts of the country we cannot ask the small business sector to expand and at the same time reach out and take $1,000 away from every family and $100 away from every senior citizen in every community, to be paid back to Ottawa, through the de-indexing process. In that event small businesses will not have a market for their goods and services.
The point we have been trying to make is that we do not have to bribe small businesses to expand through tax concessions. They will expand on their own if there is a market for their goods and services. However, in parts of Canada today the market is not there. To take millions and millions of dollars out of the communities of Canada and to ask small business to expand on their own without any market is asking small business to do too much. It is very unfair to expect them to respond to that challenge.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member began answering the questions of the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. St. Germain), he said that he welcomed the opportunity to answer questions. Now would he answer mine?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for years and years I have heard C_nadians talk about dealing with unemployment and 1 have watched with some patience the strategies that were put forward. Each time they related to stimulating the consumer, a concept which I now recognize as one aimed at creating jobs. Some of the jobs created by spending more money were the kinds where very bright young people were hired to travel around the City of Winnipeg to erect signs advertising that the project was sponsored by this Minister or that Minister. I am proud to have listened to the Budget yesterday and to have learned that the Government will no longer accept the concept that the way to create jobs is to spend money and that that stimulates the consumer.
Canadians are able to create jobs. They told us repeatedly that they wanted to stand on their own two feet. They can do so, and the Budget gives them that opportunity. 1 wish the Opposition would show as much confidence in Canadians as I think Canadians are prepared to show in themselves.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate any chance to respond to the Hon. Member's question or observation. I come from
May 24, 1985

British Columbia which has had a Conservative Government in power for some time. It had a similar approach to creating jobs in that province in terms of raising taxes and cutting back on a whole variety of government areas. I remember the advice of Michael Walker, the chief economist of the Fraser Institute. When asked in British Columbia what advice as a very wise economist he would have for young people looking for work in that province, he used a take-off on the old adage that one should go west, young man, to seek one's future, and said: "Go east, young man. Leave British Columbia and go to Manitoba because it has a different approach".
Manitoba happens to have the lowest level of unemployment in Canada. Manitoba has taken action to provide job opportunities. It has challenged the assumption that it makes sense to give young people and others UIC and welfare, to ask them to remain at home and watch television, to tell them not to provide a useful service for their communities. Manitoba had a different approach. It took the amount of money it would have spent on social services, UIC and welfare, and provided young persons with meaningful jobs so that they could serve their communities, assist senior citizens, assist single parents, provide support for daycare, playgrounds and so on. Thousands and thousands of young people in that province were mobilized and have done just that.
I come from British Columbia where that did not take place. I come from British Columbia where the Conservative Government there used a similar approach to the one in the 6.5 pounds of paper delivered last night. I know what it did for British Columbia, and I only hope and pray that the same thing will not be duplicated across the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will promise not to try and be an expert on British Columbia if the Hon. Member opposite will try not to be an expert on my province. I can state clearly that when you talk about Manitoba having the lowest level of unemployment, it is actually the second lowest. It has been the same for some time through both a Progressive Conservative and a New Democratic Party Government in Manitoba. It reflects on the people of my province, and not on the Government. If the Hon. Member is going to suggest that British Columbians were told to go east and go to Manitoba-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I'm sorry, but the period for questions and comments is now over. Resuming debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) talked about important principles. He spoke about principles that have not worked. That is why this Government has asked Canadians to follow a new road. We have made a conscious effort to break away from the tired, cynical and unsuccessful attempts of the former Government to create jobs and build a future for this country. Instead, we have forged a fresh approach in job creation, in economic prosperity and in social responsibility.
The Budget-Mrs. McDougall
The Hon. Member went on to say that Budgets are to serve people. He is absolutely right. Whay did their Budgets never serve the people? Our Budget will. It will build on the vitality and dynamism of individual Canadians and of our businesses and our industry. It is a Budget that rewards initiative. It is a Budget that reafffirms our Government's basic belief in the ability of Canadians to create the growth that in turn creates the jobs we all want and need. It is a Budget that provides Canadians with the opportunity to show their stuff, to take action and to participate in a new direction for Canada.
This has been called, in a cynical way, a Budget of faith. It is a Budget of faith because I have faith in my neighbours and in your neighbours, because I know that they will help us build the jobs that we have committed for Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
During the election, we told Canadians that we knew there was an absolute need for change to responsible fiscal management of the Government's affairs. Canadians agreed with us. We have proven that time and time again in the last eight months. We have consistently demonstrated that our policies are a break from the past. We have taken actions to reduce government overhead, streamline the programs that restrain growth, rationalize programs and eliminate waste. We talked with Canadians across the country and listened to them. Because of that, we were able to formulate our proposals with the concerns of Canadians in mind and with their ideas guiding us. We were able to benefit from views in all regions and from all sectors. In short, we were able to take advantage of perspectives from every segment of Canadian life.
I want to reiterate what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) told this House. This Budget is about jobs. It is about providing Canadians with lasting employment, with programs that are sensitive and flexible. Our actions as a Government two months after having taken office have helped create over 200,000 jobs. Despite all the doomsayers over there who said we would lose 50,000 or 100,000 jobs, we now have 200,000 jobs in this country that we did not have before.
Hon. Members know that this is a significant achievement. We know that we can do better. That is why the measures in this Budget address unemployment and the creation of employment. The Canadian people have discovered what seems to be so difficult for the opposition Parties to understand. Canadians have discovered to their pain that government spending does not create jobs, that government spending creates deficits. We have chosen not a single instrument of direct job creation. We do not believe that is responsible. By taking measures to create jobs through the capital gains tax exemption, through the training initiatives of my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), of restoring fiscal order to our balance sheets, we can create a climate of job creation of which Canadians can take advantage.
I know that debate has been occurring, especially in the pre-Budget press, over the relationship between unemployment

May 24, 1985
5050_________________________________________
The Budget-Mrs. McDougall
and the deficit, that the old pump primers still want to spend our way to full employment. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) put it more succinctly than I have ever heard it when he said several days ago "If increased deficits lowered the unemployment rate, we would have full employment this very day". The sad truth in human terms, in terms of dashed hopes of millions of Canadians, is that unemployment still remains unacceptable, despite a staggering deficit.
Clearly the Budget emphasizes fiscal responsibility, but it is not fiscal responsibility for its own sake. Such a philosophy has no place in the plans of our Government. No proposal was made, no program was changed or even considered for the sole purpose of deficit reduction. The issues at stake are too complex, too interwoven to be determined by any one narrow philosophy. The budget measures have been carefully selected and balanced to further the broad goal of economic renewal.
We are a young country, but we are carrying around a burden. That, quite frankly, is weighing us down beyond our years. It is a millstone around our neck. It is preventing the development that our economy needs. It ties the hands that create jobs and it trips the feet that are leading to the future.
There is concern for people in our deficit control action and in our efforts to restore responsibility. We have demonstrated this concern by facing the real problems that stand in the way of the better future we all desire. There is no room for wishful thinking in our policies. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) said that this is a Budget of wishful thinking. We do not wish things for small business, we give them the tools to make it happen. By bringing forward realistic effective policies, we are acting with respect for the wishes of Canadians now and with the aspirations of Canadians for today, tomorrow and the day after tomorrow.
[ Translation]
The budget is pervaded by the new spirit that has developed across this country. It is the spirit that has led our Government in its relations with the provinces, with the various sectors of our economy and with our trading partners. It is the spirit of co-operation and consultation.

Canadians know that we can each contribute in one way or another to a better Canada. That means that we must all shoulder a part of the burden. The results will take longer if we do not, and will be more difficult to obtain. The spirit is also independent. There is an enthusiasm growing across this land. I have recently been in British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Yes, the people of this country have faith in us because we have faith in them.
This Budget shows that our Government's recognition of Canadians is important. We know that Canadians know best and that Government cannot decide what is best. We are saying to Canadians, "Invest, it is your future, your children's future", and we are saying, "The Government will help you make Canada strong and prosperous". We are cutting out the red tape that strangles initiative. We are making Government
simpler, easier, more effective for Canadians who need it and for those who are working with us in the goals we have set.
The budget proposals deal with a tough reality. The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount talked about Tory times being tough times. If Tory times are tough times, it is because of the irresponsibility that has gone on for years and years before. We know we cannot give Canadians everything. We do not live in Never, Never Land. We have to act responsibly, to take control of ourselves, each of us in our own way.
I may remind the Hon. Member that we all agree that Canada must have the kind of government that will promote economic growth and stimulate development of the employment opportunities we need.
It is therefore a pleasure to be able to point to some of these programs and policies today.

At the Regina First Ministers' Conference, my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, announced a new program with an innovative approach to training and employment. This approach too is practical. It aims for career development, not just for short-term jobs. I want to emphasize that under this program, women for the first time will have access to all labour strategy programs, and one of those programs is specifically geared to women who are re-entering the workforce. Those who are most in the know, members of the local private sector, are deeply involved in this to ensure that the training meets the requirement of communities and the private sector. The Budget proposes an additional $900 million for those programs for 1986-87.
Changes proposed in the Budget assure Canadians that, for example, they will be able to enjoy the fruits of their labours. A lifetime capital gains exemption of up to half a million dollars provides significant recognition of the effort and initiative of individuals and frees up funds for investments in small and growing enterprises. This provision is not only for rich people. There is a cap on the capital gains tax exemption because it is for Canadians from all walks of life. The dry cleaner at the corner of my street at home has a modest, successful business and is ready to retire. He will be able to sell his business and keep the profits from the work he has done all his life without paying a capital gains tax.

The Budget proposals have also given full consideration to the innovative spirit of our labour organizations. A tax credit will be provided for individual investors in venture capital initiatives managed by labour organizations and which receive provincial tax assistance, such as the Solidarity Fund of the Quebec Federation of Labour.

We are all aware of the tremendous contribution played by our cultural sector in both creating jobs and preserving a vital
May 24, 1985

and rich heritage. I spoke with representatives of the Canadian Conference of the Arts this morning. They were enormously excited because, for the first time, a Finance Minister talked about the economic significance of the cultural sector and provided incentives for that sector which provides so much to our heritage and to making our country a civilized place to live. I am especially pleased by the establishment of a private sector committee in collaboration with my colleague, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse), to propose ways in which the private sector can be encouraged to increase its support for the arts.
Let us be realistic. In all sectors there is a limit to the public purse. Similarly, the proposals for pension fund investment and the RRSP changes reflect our faith in the ability of Canadians to make their own investment decisions. The pension plan proposals will encourage and strengthen private pension arrangements, will broaden the base and will give many Canadians a fair and more flexible opportunity to save for an adequate pension. Amendments to the Pension Benefits Standard Act will go forward to establish minimum standards for federally regulated pension plans. Once passed, these changes will improve the pension rights of all Canadians, and particularly those of women who make up the bulk of our part-time workforce. It will help workers who are thinking of early retirement, women in the workforce, spouses of pension plan members, and all employees. There will be improved survivor benefit regulations for women, standards for pension benefit splitting on marriage breakdown, and equality standards.
The Government believes that it must manage its own costs more effectively. The November statement initiated that process and further savings are planned in this Budget arising from additional measures to introduce more businesslike practices in the federal Government, including the sale of Crown corporations and additional cuts to government programs. In this important area, our approach has been careful, balanced and systematic. We tabled with the Budget, on behalf of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), the first report of the ministerial task force on program review. It sets out the decisions our Government has taken in this important area of government responsibility.
I am very proud to stand here today to participate in this debate with my hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance. I want to remind all Canadians of the words of that great Nova Scotian, Joseph Howe:
You are the representatives of the people and I put it to you as you are greatly honoured, should you not greatly dare?
The Budget that was placed before us yesterday by my colleague and friend, the Minister of Finance, does just that. It challenges us and dares us to take a message of hope to the people of Canada. What better place to begin that challenge than here at the heart of Canadian democracy?
Hon. Members opposite, in their quiet and reflective moments, share the Government's concern about the situation which we inherited on September 4. The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount knows that this is true. He spoke
The Budget-Mrs. McDougall
eloquently today and I listened with interest as he spoke because I recall his words last year when he said:
Anyone who tells you, you don't have to face up to those hard choices (in spending cuts) would be better off as a tour guide in Disneyland. Any major new government programs can only come at the expense of existing ones. We must not mortgage our children's future by going deeper and deeper into debt.
The Hon. Member was right. The Government has taken that responsibility seriously. It has taken its responsibility seriously not only to care for those who need our help in today's world but enable our children and those who follow us to hope, to plan, and yes, to dare. I recall what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said to a high school student last year. He said, "Your generation is going to be strangled if Ottawa continues to go into debt at the current pace". He too was correct.
We sense the frustration in Canada but we are a Party of optimists. We believe in the future and we believe in tomorrow. We believe we can embrace tomorrow only if we act with responsibility today. We are the trustees of tomorrow and we are determined not to let tomorrow's greatness escape our beneficiaries.
I look to my friends opposite, and they are my friends because I have established a great deal of respect for them, and I ask them, where is their logic, their sense of responsibility? The NDP's own policy advisers have told them that they have been left with an economic analysis of little value and an economic program that is a hodgepodge of contradictions and dead-end solutions. With all due respect I say to Hon. Members, wake up and smell the coffee. Even their colleagues are uncertain about their formula.
I remember how heartened 1 was to hear the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) earlier this spring state on national television as he looked straight into the camera, "We can't simply accept that we have large deficits continuing ... it does not make sense". Hear, hear, I thought. Finally there has been a conversion of this Party like the one on the road to Damascus. However, after hearing once again the same tired cliches emanating from the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shus-wap, I can see that that was a conversion for the cameras only.
Thus I wish to conclude by asking Hon. Members to take into account Mr. Howe's question in addressing this Budget: should we not greatly dare?
[ Translation]
And why should we not?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does the Minister believe that having corporation taxes go down by half a billion dollars and individual taxes going up by $1 billion next year is fair? As well, does she consider it fair that those who were legally able to avoid paying any income tax last year will not pay a minimum tax this year and that the surcharge has no effect on them whatsoever? Does she believe those two things to be fair?

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mrs. McDougall

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the Budget we indicated that we recognize that corporation taxes need a thorough review. We have published a paper on how choices can be made to reform corporation taxes. In addition, we have placed a tax on financial institutions. Also, we have eliminated some of the loopholes to which the Hon. Member referred, such as using hotels under certain circumstances. Some other loopholes have been removed, such as the scientific research tax credit. We have moved to ensure that the system will become fair. We will continue to do that. It is a continuing program. It is not something which will stop today, it will go on. We will be looking at the whole taxation system through corporation taxes. We know that there are still changes to be made and we will be making them. Some were made in November and some are being made now.
What the Hon. Member is forgetting is that the people of Canada who will benefit from some of the things which we have done will not be the rich and wealthy Canadians. Those who will benefit will be small-businessmen and farmers. Has he forgotten about the farmers? They are the ones who will benefit the most from some of the things which we have done. It will be easier for them to pass on their farms to the next generation.
It is a fair Budget. Fair means that Canadians can look us in the eye, as they have been doing today. We have been flooded with telephone calls and letters from the people of Canada who are saying that they agree with the Budget and that they know we are on the right track.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a couple of questions to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). In January, the Department of Finance published a paper entitled Tax Issues in Agriculture. That paper indicated that farmers earn twice as much as the average Canadian and that they only pay a quarter of the taxes which ordinary Canadians pay. It also indicated that farmers were approximately eight times better off than the average Canadian. The response to that paper from the agricultural community was swift and predictable. It absolutely slaughtered the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on his view of the world and on his view of the Canadian farming scene. It is little wonder!
On October 30, 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation published a paper which indicated that 17 per cent of Canadian farmers were in serious financial difficulty. That paper was referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. A few weeks later, the committee released a report which completely rejected the position of the Minister of Finance. If anything, the farm debt crisis in Canada has deepened. A report from an agriculture committee in Bruce County indicated that it was not 17 per cent, but that 30 per cent of the farmers were in serious financial difficulty in countries such as Bruce and Grey.
The report of the standing committee, which had a majority of Tory Members, recommended an emergency program of agri-bonds which would address the serious financial difficulties which some 39,000 farmers face in Canada. That recommendation provided for long-term, low interest agri-bonds at 8 per cent for a five-year period, up to a maximum of $300,000.
The Minister spoke about what the Budget would do for farmers. Certainly, it does not address the serious financial difficulties of the 39,000 farmers who are facing foreclosure or bankruptcy this year. If there is any urgency in the agricultural community, it is that urgency. The Budget, as far as I can see, does not address the situation. I am wondering why the Government did not adopt the recommendation of the standing committee which would have dealt with the serious financial difficulties which face 39,000 farmers. It would have provided long-term, low interest rate loans from the Farm Credit Corporation with a view to saving the farms of those producers who are the most productive. Those producers are the youngest and produce one-half of the produce in Canada. Why did the Budget not deal with that matter? Why did the Government not accept the report of the Standing Committee of Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Party is well aware and very sensitive to the problems which face farmers in Canada, particularly those farmers who are struggling to hang on to their farms and those who have faced the most difficulty. We do have policies for those farmers. However, it is not part of the budgetary process; it is part of a review which is now before the Minister of Finance. He recognizes the sensitivity in the area and he knows, as we all do, that this segment is very important to Canada. Therefore, he will review the policies with respect to farmers.
Some farmers will benefit from proposals concerning the red meat stabilization plan. Other farmers will benefit from the expansion of the small business bond. Sixty per cent of small business bonds go to the agricultural community.
We know farmers are facing problems and we are reviewing those problems. We will be coming forward with policies for farmers. Some of the policies which help the farmers of Canada are in the Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister to tell all Canadians today who is responsible for the situation in which the Canadian Government now finds itself. I think it is important because for hours on end we are going to be listening to the great Liberal tenors blaming us for everything under the sun, searching for every kind of discrepancy, and posing as the self-appointed defenders of the poor, the underprivileged, the elderly. They ought to hang their heads in shame, and I would like the Minister to set the record straight today and tell all Canadians who are listening who in fact is responsible for the present situation in Canada.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Conservatives, my friend! You have brought forth a Budget which falls far short of the mark.
May 24, 1985

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yes, we all know who is responsible for the situation in which elderly Canadians find themselves today. Pension reform was studied for 10 years and we were able to make good use of what was accomplished by the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) when he was involved with pensions. We thank him for that. It is too had that after all that time the situation had to wait for us to take action.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is still less than 24 hours since the unveiling of the Conservative Budget. With the exception of Investment Canada, it is the first piece of legislation which came directly from this Government. It gives us a clear statement of its policy and its view of Canada.
We have already heard an overwhelming amount of critical comment on the budget proposals which strike directly at low and middle-income families. The reaction is real and it is justified. Ordinary taxpayers are the target of the Government's efforts to raise revenue. For many months we heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) talk about a mythical bank president, or a mother who was receiving family benefits which she did not really need. But it seems that if the Government has aimed at the bank president in this budget, it has shot the teller.
Lower-income Canadians will be paying dearly. A two-parent family with two children and one income totalling $20,000 will be paying upwards of $350 extra in taxes, and that figure does not include the losses from de-indexation of family tax benefits and tax deductions.
Low and middle-income earners will be paying but what are they being offered by the Government? Will all these tax increases and discriminatory measures produce more jobs for our 1.4 million unemployed? The budget does not say so. In this budget, the Government is forcing the average Canadian to pay, and to accept in return a vague promise of better times to come. I say a "vague promise" because the budget has no agenda for economic growth and no projections for growth beyond next year.
I understand that the Department of Finance has prepared forecasts for five years and further but they were not used. In the budget document on Canada's Economic Prospects for 1985-1990, most tables stop at 1986. We are not told what the Government expects the eventual impact of its budget proposals to be. Impact statements have been asked for and have been refused. We are simply told to shoulder this extra tax burden and soldier on.
Canadians are overwhelmingly concerned about unemployment and the Government has not adequately addressed that concern in this budget. Without an agenda for economic growth, who can guarantee any improvement in the unemplo-ment situation? Again, in the Minister's own budget papers, he shows GNP for 1985 at 3.1 as compared to 4.7 in 1984. It shows GNP in 1986 at 2.4. In other words, the Minister's own
The Budget-Miss Nicholson
figures are showing a loss of economic growth. The same table shows unemployment figures of 11.1 in 1984 and 10.3 in 1986.
There is a further statement which adds to our confusion. It says that in 1985, consumption is expected to be an important source of growth. Yet we have measures here which are going to reduce the purchasing power of Canadians. The Government shows a 10.3 per cent unemployment level in 1986, which is still unacceptably high. Are we to take it that the Government is satisfied with the 10 per cent unemployment rate? Is that what Canadians have to look forward to as a result of this anti-family, anti-consumer budget?
When I questioned the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) earlier today on these matters, he said that numbers are not the be-all and end-all of budgets. It is interesting to note that he was somewhat reluctant to discuss the figures from his own Department. However, in a way, the Minister is correct. Budgets are less about numbers of more about people because it is the ordinary working, middle and low-income people who pay taxes, who buy things and who keep the economy going. But here we have a budget which is going to take billions of dollars of purchasing power out of the economy. At the same time we are asked to accept the promise that the unemployment rate will be reduced. Yet we know that even to stay where we are in terms of our present unacceptable 11 per cent rate of unemployment, we need economic growth of 3 per cent. The Government is projecting a loss of economic growth. It is also projecting a slight drop in unemployment. That does not make sense, Mr. Speaker.
Let us leave the numbers for a moment and consider expectations. What might Canadians have expected to see in this budget given the promises of the Government? First, let us consider fairness. The budget amounts to a series of tax breaks for big business and tax grabs from middle and low-income families. Is that to be considered a definition of fairness? The sales tax is not only increased but the number of items which are subject to sales tax is greatly enlarged and includes such necessities of life as soap and medical supplies. This is going to be particularly hard on families with young children and low incomes.
The Government promised a minimum tax on the wealthy. This is not delivered. We have another discussion paper. The temporary surtax is certainly not to be confused with the minimum tax on the wealthy because the temporary surtax applies only to people with taxable income. If, indeed, one has a clever accountant who can guarantee that one has no taxable income, then ovbiously the surtax does not apply. So the minimum tax on the wealthy is another promise which was not kept.
With respect to pensions for home makers, I might just mention that the Government's pension proposals, as far as they go and in so far as they are laudable, are a rehash of reforms introduced by the previous Liberal Government. But this Government did not follow through with the Liberal proposal to provide protection from inflation in private pension benefits, and the Government did not come through with any proposals on pensions for homemakers even though the Prime

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Miss Nicholson
Minister campaigned on a promise to institute home maker's pensions.
With respect to maintaining universal social programs, I must say we have come a very long way since universality was regarded as a sacred trust. Before Christmas there were threats that all social programs were up for review and might be rearranged. This Party led the criticism and, indeed, Canada's citizens protested loud and hard. So the Government backed off and watered down its consultation paper. This is the same Government which, when in opposition, howled in outrage when old age benefits were capped at 6 and 5 per cent, even though the resultant drop in inflation meant that the pensioners lost only $2.17 while the caps were in place. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), and those others of us who were here, will certainly remember the howls of outrage because capping was occurring at six and five, but what we now see essentially is de-indexed pensions and family allowances.
This Budget is mean spirited and puts pensioners and families in the undignified position of being participants in a pension and family allowance lottery. If inflation is hovering at, say, 2.9 per cent, they will just have to hope that inflation nudges over 3 per cent so that their benefits will be indexed and they will have a better chance of making ends meet. What does that say about the attitude of the Government toward its retired labour force and those who are raising a future labour force?
While we are exploring attitudes, let us look at the $500,000 capital gains deduction. In introducing that change the Minister made it sound very reasonable. He spoke of the retiring farmer, and I think we would all sympathize with the idea that someone who is retiring, having worked hard on the farm or in a small business, might indeed get a break on capital gains and be able to plan to invest sensibly for retirement after a long life of hard and productive work. But we look again at the Budget papers and nothing limits the application of this exemption in any way. It could be applied to someone who has fine arts, jewellery bought in Switzerland, or a condominium in the Caribbean. There is no way that this is particularly aimed at the productive members of the Canadian economy. It can be used by someone who has no intention of contributing to the Canadian economy. This is really a slap in the face for the majority of Canadians who are doing what they can in these difficult times and who are now being asked to bear the brunt of the Government's tax increases.
Let us look at what is happening with energy. We find a tax levied which is being described as 2 cents a litre. In fact, if one adds in some other things resulting from the Western Accord,
1 think it is more likely to be 2.8 cents per litre. The Government's own figures in the Budget papers concerning the anticipated revenue from this gas hike just about matched the revenue it has lost by cancelling the PGRT. In other words, the multinationals get a gift and ordinary Canadians pay. I say "multinationals" advisedly, because those who benefited from
the PGRT were the multinationals who had old oil; the smaller Canadian companies with more recent exploration did not benefit. So the Government has chosen to help the multinationals and ask the ordinary Canadian to pay.
As well, paying for energy involves much more than paying at the gas pump or paying more to heat one's house. There is an energy cost in practically everything we use. Energy costs are included all through the food chain in things such as transportation, processing, packaging, storage and marketing. Therefore, as a result of this quite substantial hike in gasoline prices, we can certainly expect food prices to go up.
There are other elements in this Budget which are also inflationary and that have not been faced squarely either. I fully expect that during the coming days, as we plough our way through this six pounds of paper, we will find many more things to comment on. But the single important point I want to make is that this Budget has failed to address questions of economic growth. Without growth we will not have new jobs. There is in fact a great risk that this Government, which is so concerned about the deficit, may have put so many regressive measures in place here that they will choke recovery and we will end up with a higher deficit.
I would just like to comment on a statement by the Minister of Finance after he came to power. In December of 1984, when the Department of Finance, which had predicted growth of 3.8 per cent, revised its figures and projected economic growth to 1990 would decline to an annual average of 3.2 per cent per year, the Minister of Finance said this is not an acceptable outlook for Canadians. That was a very clear statement. Yet here we have in the Budget papers a projection of 2.4 per cent for 1986, which is even worse, but apparently the Minister now finds that acceptable. Had he found it unacceptable, then surely his Budget would have included measures to raise that growth rate substantially within the same time-frame.
What we are talking about, Mr. Speaker, is the definition of our economic problems and the clarity of thought underlying how they are dealt with. This is where one has to be worried about a fixation on the deficit. Of course the deficit is important, but it is one factor and a symptom, not a cause. I get very worried when I find the whole emphasis on the deficit and apparently not much concern about the $50 billion worth of goods and services we are not producing but could be, and the need to get this economy more vibrant and active. That I think is the real issue; how to get more economic growth, more jobs. That is the best way to get the deficit down and 1 do not think that has been touched by this Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first like to say how pleased I am to be taking part in this historic debate. I would like to thank as well as congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) on behalf of the people of my riding of Niagara Falls for setting a clear direction for the economic recovery of this country. The Budget will be welcomed by individuals from my riding, and I believe that it will also be welcomed by all Canadians.
May 24, 1985

Many people have written to me from my riding, as well as from across the country. Most of them have said the same thing; they want the Government of Canada to continue with those themes that we talked about as candidates in the 1984 election campaign. They want us to be true to our word and do everything we can to encourage job creation. They know, and 1 think most Members of this House will agree whether they admit it or not, that job creation will only be possible in Canada when the Government of Canada puts its own economic house in order and frees up the entrepreneurial spirit in Canadians to create more jobs. I believe this Budget makes that theme very, very clear.
As the Hon. Minister of Finance said last night, it is a Budget which rewards success rather than subsidizing effort. It is a Budget which builds on the sense of co-operation which this Government has created among all levels of government and the private sector; co-operation which is so necessary to our economy. This Budget, once and for all, puts an end to the fallacy that the federal Government alone can create all the jobs necessary to cure our country's unemployment. It is true that, given co-operation among all the players in Canadian society, Canada will once again be healthy economically.
I believe the Budget introduced last night by the Minister of Finance will do three things to set the course for Canada's economic recovery. First, and finally, after years of Government overspending and misspending, we will control and ultimately reduce the national debt. Second, we will improve the effectiveness and management of all areas of the federal Government. Third, we will encourage private initiatives by increasing the availability of capital and start rewarding success. This is the mandate that I believe we were given on September 4.
In my opinion the staggering growth of the national deficit has for many years hindered real growth in our econony. We have recognized that the first step in long-term regeneration is the control of the national deficit. The Budget of yesterday afternoon and the November statement are the first significant steps in that direction in 15 years. I was, therefore, pleased when the Minister of Finance announced that the deficit for this fiscal year will be $4.4 billion less than it would have been had no action been taken. The deficit for this fiscal year will be $33.8 billion as opposed to $38.2 billion.
This process will continue in the fiscal year 1986-87. According to predictions the deficit will be $8.3 billion less, down to $32.7 billion, as opposed to $40.2 billion. Most significantly, the direct impact of all these efforts since the Government has taken office is to reduce the deficit in 1990 by $20 billion. 1 am sure that all Canadians congratulate the Minister of Finance for producing a medium-term strategy that will ensure that the national deficit will be $75 billion less by 1990 than if no action had been taken.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I believe that the necessity of reducing our national debt is recognized not only by those individuals who voted for the Progressive Conservative Party, but by the Members of the two Opposition Parties as well. All of us remember when early last spring the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) made just that point. He said that if he were elected Prime Minister of Canada he would reduce the structural debt in the country by 50 per cent over the course of seven years. He recognized what we are talking about in this Budget. As far back as 1982 the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) as well made the same statement. He said that the national deficit was too high. To that extent 1 believe they agree that we are making the right moves.
The theme of deficit reduction has been a theme of the Progressive Conservative Party for some time. This subject came up very often during the recent federal election campaign. I made the point, and I know others agreed with me and made similar points, that the country would never again be healthy economically until the national deficit was reduced. If big deficits and uncontrolled spending could have solved the unemployment problem in Canada, every man, woman, and child in the country would have two jobs by now.
There will be those in the Opposition ranks who will disagree with our approach. They will say that efforts at reducing of the national deficit are unfair and unwise at this time. They will make essentially the same speeches they made last November after the presentation of the economic statement. The arguments I heard earlier this afternoon are the same ones I heard in Novemver. After the economic statement the NDP said that we will lose jobs. Other people said that interest rates and inflation will go up. In fact, since November we have seen the creation of 200,000 new jobs. Interest rates today are at their lowest level in a decade. Inflation has come down and investor confidence has risen. The record of predictions of those who will criticize the approach will be as good as it was last November. They were wrong in November and are wrong again in May.
As I mentioned earlier, in order for the Government to create new jobs in Canada it is necessary for the Government to put its own affairs in order. It must improve the effectiveness and management of Government, the Public Service, and its policy with respect to Crown corporations. I believe there is no clearer statement as to where the Government intends to go than that made last night on the subject of Crown corporations. This is consistent with what we said in the past election campaign. It is our belief that unless a Crown corporation fulfills a continuing public policy purpose it should be sold. Government must return to the private sector activities which properly belong there.
In November the Government announced its intentions to sell the assets of the Canada Development Investment Corporation, including its holdings in Canadair and de Havilland. It is estimated that the sale of these companies will reduce the cash requirement of the Government of Canada by approximately $675 million and the federal deficit by some $350 million in 1985-86.

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson
In addition, Mr. Speaker, corporations that no longer serve public purposes are being wound up. Legislation has already been introduced in Parliament to wind up the Canada Sports Pool Corporation, Loto Canada, and others. As well, five other corporations which are inactive, including Uranium Canada Limited and Mingan Associates, are being wound up.
The days when Government can afford to subsidize the mistakes of the past are over and that is a good thing for all of Canada. The business of Government is not business, it is to give direction to business. The Government will no longer pretend to be an entrepreneur. Decisions in this area are difficult, but they must be made. This is very true in the case of Cape Breton Island.
Although I was born in Niagara Falls and am very proud to represent the people of Niagara Falls, I continue to have hundreds of relatives on Cape Breton Island. When I visited there recently I overhead a discussion about the heavy water plants on Cape Breton Island. One individual made the point that these companies are costing the people of Canada approximately $100 million a year to keep 600 people employed. They are producing a product for which there is no longer a market. He said that he did not believe anyone had the courage to do what must be done, to day that enough is enough. He was proven wrong yesterday. The Government has the courage to say that the mistakes of the past cannot continue.
1 was pleased to hear that, in addition to making that tough decision, the Government will not abandon the people of Cape Breton. Workers at that plant will receive generous severance benefits and will be assisted in seeking new employment elsewhere. An enriched tax incentive for new investment is being introduced and all new investment in that part of the country will be free of corporate income tax for 10 years.
In addition to our policy of privatization of Crown corporations, the Budget sets out a number of additional internal measures that we are taking to increase the effectiveness with which taxpayers' money is spent. The Public Service pension plan will be put on a fully funded basis with no taxpayer subsidy. The guarantee of indexation of pensions of Members of Parliament and Senators will end January 1, 1986. An aggressive program is being put into place to improve the Government's management of its cash and to dispose of property that it no longer needs. Most significantly, the federal Public Service, which was expected to increase in size by 15,000 positions over the next six years, will in fact be decreased by 15,000 positions.
As a result of these measures and those taken in November the Government will save more than $2 billion this year. That figure will grow to over $3 billion by 1990. The Government will also encourage private initiative. The Government realizes that this country was built on the strength of the individual and the courage of the small business person. For too many years we have said that Government can do it all. This has been demonstrated many times to be wrong for our country. The Government should encourage investment and risk-taking and reward success.
In order to encourage more Canadians to invest in Canada's growth, the Government is proposing a lifetime capital gains exemption of $500,000 for individuals. This lifetime exemption will be phased in over five years beginning this year. The full $500,000 exemption will be available to farmers immediately in recognition of their special problems and their contributions to Canadian society. I take particular pleasure in that provision in the Budget. Many times the farmers in my area from Niagara-on-the-Lake and Virgil have made that exact point to me. They would like to acquire new farmland, pass their farms on or dispose of their lands as they saw fit without the burden of capital gains. I was particularly pleased to see that measure in the Budget.
I believe the initiative taken by the Government in this area of capital gains will encourage entrepreneurship and investment by individual Canadians in their country. The Government is saying, "We want Canadians to invest. We want Canadians to build and create jobs. We want Canadians to be successful". It has been estimated that almost 1 million Canadians make capital gains, a vast majority of whom earn less than $40,000. This capital gains incentive is a strong signal that the new Government wants people with good ideas and the will to persevere to enjoy the fruits of their success. The Government of Canada is confident that Canadians will accept that challenge.
Small and medium sized businesses will also benefit from our proposals to change regulations governing RRSPs and pension fund investments. These measures will allow greater investment by pension funds in new businesses and small businesses seeking to expand. The measure will enable people with RRSPs to invest the plans directly in smaller Canadian businesses.
Small businesses and farmers will benefit from the extension of the small business farm program until 1987, and small businesses will be exempted for one year from the 5 per cent corporate surtax in recognition of the importance of strengthening small business and facilitating job creation. New and growing research and development companies will be entitled to a direct refund of the full tax credit that they earn on their first $2 million of R and D each year. Action will be taken to make the system fairer and to improve tax administration. These actions will benefit all of us, but especially entrepreneurs and small business owners by reducing administrative headaches.
Last night we saw a Budget that balanced tax fairness, effective Government management and the encouragement of private initiative. In order to accomplish those goals we all know that tough medicine is required. Last night someone in my apartment building approached me and said, "I think it is a good Budget but I am sorry that drinkers and smokers have to be taxed." I am sorry about a lot of things, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry that for 18 years we had a Government that overspent and misspent taxpayers' money. I am sorry that we built airports to which no one wanted to fly and that we build planes

that nobody wanted to buy. I am sorry about all those things. This redoubles my commitment and the commitment of the Conservative Party to do something about the mistakes of the past and to make a clear statement that the Government alone cannot solve the problems of this country.
I believe the Budget contains a number of actions that will be taken to ensure greater fairness in the tax system. Specifically there will be a minimum income tax imposed on upper income Canadians in place in time for the 1986 taxation year. This I know is a concern to Canadians. I think most of us realize that we have to pay tax, but all of us want to have the assurance that everyone will pay his or her fair share.
