subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been an amazing circus criss-crossing the country over the last week or so trying to add some new buzz words to the political vocabulary of Canada-tough but fair, tough but fair. They hit the headlines, they hit the newscasts. They seem to have hit everything except the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) because what he brought in was a tough luck Budget. It is a Budget which is hard on Canadians. It is a Budget which is hard on the people who make up my constituency and the constituencies of every Member of the House of Commons. It is a Budget which is anything but fair. It is a Budget which is unjust. It is a Budget which is typified by the fact that our finance critic, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), could read portions from the Lalonde Budget and have the Conservatives clapping, thinking it was their Budget which they were supporting. It is a Budget in the sorry, sad and failed tradition of the Liberal Government which went before this Government.
I had hoped-I must say against hope, but I am an eternal optimist-that the Government would have learned its lesson after November, that it would have learned that the Liberal Party approach of cut-backs and of a fatuous concern with the deficit is an approach that will lead us to disaster.
I stood in my place in the House of Commons after the November statement and I predicted-and I ask Hon. Members to check the words which I stated at that stage-that in fact the budget changes which were brought in then, because they had the effect of decreasing economic activity in the country, would increase the budget deficit. Everybody looked quite amazed and thought that that could not happen. However, when the Minister of Finance stood yesterday, he conceded that the budget deficit is now $36 billion, not $35 billion as he projected.
The reason is absolutely clear. It is that economic activity has been slowed. Investment has not had the kind of expansion and buoyancy that this Government expected to occur, by magic. Instead we have had a perpetuation of an unemployment rate that is shameful for any country to experience. We have an unemployment rate 4 percentage points above that the United States. The unemployment rate is not significantly decreasing. It is an unemployment rate that persists, and we have a deficit that is rising. That is precisely what we predicted would be the consequence of the November statement, which followed the wrongheaded policies of the previous regime. Rather than accepting the lessons that we so magnanimously offer, these misguided souls on the Treasury benches continue in their misguided ways. They do so with a particular sense of affrontery as far as this Budget is concerned.
The Budget-Mr. Langdon
There is a level of unemployment in this country which our action group on jobs, as it criss-crossed across this country, heard described in place after place, community after community, as a human tragedy, a tragedy that was destroying the hopes and expectations of our young people. It is a tragedy that is putting into the ashcan of our society the older workers.
I presented a petition this morning from people in Kitchener, people who represent older workers, those over 40 and older. They do not have the prospect, as things stand in this country, to find jobs for themselves. The tragedy is very much there.
Forlorn optimist that I am, I expected that somehow there would be within this Budget something to permit the poor back-benchers to defend it as they go back to their constituencies this weekend, so that they would be able to point and say "There is a community initiatives fund that we have set up to assist communities to get people back to work. There is a youth initiatives fund to permit young people to start up their own businesses. There is something that would assist agriculture". Perhaps there could be the kind of thing we suggested in our group report. $100 million to help soil conservation measures in agriculture or the $200 million that we suggested to support reforestation in this country. I did not expect that would be the thrust of the Budget.
I have listened to the rhetoric of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Being the Prime Minister, I certainly thought we could believe him. He is a clever politician. I thought that within the Budget he would have inserted some gestures, some symbols of concern about the vast number of people out of work in this country. Granted, they might just be symbols; $200 million for a community initiatives fund instead of the $850 million that we recommended. I thought there might have been a limited amount for agriculture and a limited amount in terms of support for industrial renewal. I searched.
Yesterday I sat in on the lock-up. I figured it would be a difficult Budget to analyze. I thought within it there would be symbols or gestures and that it would be difficult for us as opposition people to make our way past some of the gestures to find the real substance of the Budget. In fact, this Government made it easy for us. It set before this House a Budget which, believe it or not, in a country with 10.9 per cent of the population out of work, does not have a single initiative to put people back to work directly. There is not a single initiative or a gesture to help, for example, get 20,000 people back into the workforce. There is not a single initiative to help people in agriculture.
I feel for the back-benchers who will face criticism from those in their constituencies who will be out of work over the next eight months, indeed the next 18 months. As a politician, I find it unbelievable that a Government would bring in a Budget that has in cold black print, which each of us will circulate as widely as possible throughout this country, a projection, and I refer to the Government's statistics in Table 5 of Canada's Economic Prospects, that 18 months from now, in December 1986, there will still be 10.3 per cent of the workforce in this country out of work.

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mr. Langdon
In the course of a year and a half this Budget has set itself the heroic goal of cutting the rate of unemployment in this country by .6 per cent. Congratulations to those on the Treasury benches. I admire their political courage. They have guts indeed to stand before the country and say that this is a Budget about jobs when their own figures tell us that in 18 months the unemployment rate will have been reduced by .6 of a percentage point, and that with the most incredible of assumptions.
When you start as an economist instead of a politician to look at the assumptions that lie behind this Budget, you find they are assumptions behind which no independent economist with whom I am acquainted in this country would be prepared to stand. They are assumptions that suggest that growth rates inthe United States are going to continue to be quite positive for the next two years. We know from United States statistics that there is a significant downturn in economic activity occurring in the United States which makes those figures laughable, pie in the sky.
At the same time, if you look at the figures for investment next year in this country, which are plugged into this Budget, you see the bizarre prediction that there will be a real increase in investment in this country next year of 6.4 per cent in non-residential investment. Incredibly, it will be 10.7 per cent for residential investment. This is to happen at the same time as consumer expenditures in this country go up, according to the Government's own statistics, by 1.1 per cent.
I would hate to suggest that the Minister of Finance needs to return to first-year economics. I would hate to suggest that he needs a better understanding of the very basic laws of investment in any country. However, I would ask the Conservative back-benchers who come from the business community, if they were to face in cold, hard print the Government's prediction that there will be an increase of only 1 per cent in consumer spending, would they make vast new investments? Would they put their hard earned cash into risky business ventures in the hopes that they would be successful? I assume that Conservative back-benchers recognize, as Conservative front-benchers do not, that businesses need customers.
The Government would have us believe that people will rush out next year to put 10.7 per cent more investment into residential investment and 6.4 per cent more into non-residential investment, while at the same time consumers will only spend 1 per cent more. That is absolutely laughable. It is indefensible to anyone from the Conservative back-benches who has a degree in economics or at the very least has been in business for some years.
I plead with Conservative back-benchers to take the Minister of Finance aside and explain to him the facts of life. Tell him how the business world works, explain to him and the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) that across this country, small businesses want to know that they will have customers and that there will be a market for what they produce before they invest. I beg them to go to him. I would
not ask them to do so publicly, as I do not want them to get into trouble.

There is absolutely nothing to provide a counterweight to the price Cape Breton is required to carry.
We have before us a Budget which is totally, and bizarrely inaccurate. It is a Budget which is based on dreams. It suggests to me that the Minister of Finance must be about to bring forth a Bill to legalize marijuana. It seems to me that this Budget was brought forth in a haze of dreams. It is a Budget built on fraud, on myth and on a total misunderstanding of how the small business community works. We have a Budget which hammers the people of this country.
It is estimated that in Essex County average families will pay an extra $500 in tax this year as a result of this Budget, and will pay nine cents more per gallon of gas. When their kids go to get soft drinks at the store they will have to pay federal sales tax. When the wives buy makeup they will have to pay federal sales tax. Medicine and health products are being taxed. There has been a big jump in taxes on beer, cigarettes, liquor and wine. Sales taxes on all goods are going up. Via Rail is going to raise its fares at least 30 per cent in the Windsor to Quebec City corridor. There will be an income tax increase of at least $215 per family. This is coming from a Government that promised it would not bring in increases in income tax.
What we have before us is a Budget that, in economic terms, is a hopeless disaster, and in human terms in an unfair burden imposed upon the people of this country.
There has not been one single specific move to put a minimum tax into effect. There will be a decrease of $540 million in corporation taxes for next year while individual taxes will go up $1 billion or even more by 1991. We have a Budget that hurts the resource sector through cut-backs in agriculture and fisheries. It is a Budget that hurts the industrial sector through cut-backs to IRDP.
To conclude, it is a Budget that fails completely to meet the hopes and expectations about which we heard across the country as our action group spoke to hundreds and hundreds of groups of Canadians. The Government talks about consultation. We actually consulted instead of just playing the game. What we heard led to a budget proposal entitled Canada Unlimited which contains a real set of benefits for Canadians, not the kind of damage that this Budget invites.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really very pleased that the Hon. Member reminded us once again that he is an
May 24, 1985

economics professor. I know who should go back to take the first-year course in economics.
We in this country have experienced some of the things recommended by the Hon. Member like the Youth Initiative Fund. These are little funds in little pots. What has this left us? It has left us with huge deficit and unemployment. While the Hon. Member was speaking of all the funny-money economics at which he seems to be so expert, the Hon. Member for Guelph (Mr. Winegard) was meeting with 40 senior citizens in the lobby of this very building. These senior citizens commended the Government for its Budget.
How can the Hon. Member reconcile what he said today with the statement he made while smiling into the television camera earlier this spring? At that time he said we can't simply accept continuing large deficits; that does not make sense. There are only two ways to reduce the debt of this nation; reduce expenditures and increase taxes. Does the Hon. Member have another suggestion?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in fact 70 suggestions which were put together in the proposal entitled Canada Unlimited. I would argue that it contains an approach which recognizes reality. The reality is that we now have a deficit of $36 billion, not because the previous Government set out to achieve that level of deficit, but because it bought exactly the same kind of crazy, mixed up logic of which this Government is speaking. The Government thinks that if it cuts back, raises taxes and relies on the corporate sector, it will put people back to work and bring down the deficit.
Earlier today we had the quite dramatic spectacle of Conservatives clapping vigorously for phrases which came out of the Liberal Budget of Marc Lalonde. The reason for that is absolutely clear. That Liberal Budget did exactly the same thing. It tried to cut the deficit and the result was an increase in the deficit.
I would like to make it very clear that Canada cannot afford over the next three to five years to keep building deficits. It is not fair to future generations if we spend 30 per cent of what we take from the taxpayers of the country to service the public debt. It is wrong and morally indefensible. If we want to do something about that burden, there is only one way to do it.
When I commented on the November statement, I predicted, because of the cut-backs and the tax increases, that the deficit would be higher than $35 billion. Was I right? I was absolutely right. The deficit is now $36 billion. I will make exactly the same prediction today. The Government thinks it will reduce the deficit by squeezing the economy. The result will be a higher deficit. The people in the Treasury benches will help to bankrupt the country. They will have to carry the responsibility in the years ahead. There is a single answer. [Translation]
There is only one solution, and it must be one that will provide for a growing economy.
The Budget-Mr. Langdon

It is necessary to have an economy which will grow fast. This economy, as a result of the actions of the Government, will not grow, it will decrease. In 1985 there will be a growth rate of 3.1 per cent, and in 1986 the growth rate will be 2.4 per cent. The Government is driving the country into disaster, as the Liberal Party did before it. As a result, we will end up with a higher deficit. Members on the other side of the House will be to blame for that.
The answer is to bring into effect what the NDP presented six weeks ago. We need a significant change in the tax system which would require the corporate sector to pay its fair share, instead of decreasing corporate taxes which this Budget does. We need a change which would put a permanent fair tax burden on wealthy Canadians. It should be permanent, not a one-shot surtax. At the same time, we should be providing tax relief for ordinary Canadians. We should be providing tax benefits for working people. The working people should not have the tax loads which they will be required to pay as as result of this irresponsibility.
If we put the significant amount of money we would get as a result of those changes into community initiatives and provided help for young people, communities, the housing industry and municipalities, people could return to work. The unemployment rate would be cut by 2.5 per cent, not by the .6 per cent about which the Government seems ecstatic. I would warn government Members, when they go out into the country to defend a target or a prediction, that over the next 18 months the unemployment rate will only be reduced by .06 per cent. Those Members will come back to the House with red faces their tails between their legs. As a result, I hope a new Budget will be brought down within three months.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that question has been raised. In fact, there are so many targets in the Budget that I did not want to touch on all of them. A most destructive, senseless and ridiculous approach has been taken in the Budget. At a time when we are trying to save energy and, indeed, as the Members said, to encourage people to convert to alternate energy sources, the Budget has placed a federal sales tax on wood burning stoves, wind deflectors, heat pumps, solar heaters, panels for furnaces, insulation materials, wind generators, windmills, wind deflectors and other such goods. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today is a great day because I have been given an opportunity to defend an excellent Budget, and it is also a day I have been waiting for ever since I became a Member of this House, because today I am making my maiden speech in this House.
The Budget brought down yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Member for Etobicoke Centre, is of paramount importance. It constitutes a turning point, a totally new economic direction that the Government of Canada is obliged to take, without delay. We have turned the page. The economic situation in Canada had become critical and reducing the deficit was both necessary and urgent. This was due to the following, and I would like to quote what the Minister said in his speech, and I quote:
High deficits constrain our ability to promote growth and create jobs. High unemployment in turn contributes to even higher deficits.
Canada was caught in a situation from which it could be freed only by taking a totally different approach. This Budget addresses the vicious circle of unemployment and debt, which was spiralling upwards at a terrifying rate.
This Budget's philosophy is to urge Canadians to take the initiative and to become the instrument of our country's economic renewal. It was important to allow the private sector substantial room for manoeuvring, because the State cannot act as an absolute power and constantly tell its citizens what they must do. Canadians want jobs and they want permanent jobs. However, it is not up to the Government alone to create jobs. All Canadian men and women must help make it happen: small businesses, medium-sized businesses, big corporations and the Government. In this context, the new measures being proposed are very definite incentives. That is why, Mr. Speaker, as the Member for the riding of Louis-Hebert, it is with great pride that I rise in the House today to speak to the concerns of my constituents who, I am sure, will understand the sound reasoning behind these budgetary measures.
I would like to describe, very briefly, my riding which is located on the shores of the St. Lawrence and includes four towns, Sainte-Foy being the largest with a population of 70,000. My riding also includes Sillery, Cap-Rouge and L'An-cienne-Lorette, which are not as big and together have a population of 100,000. Sainte-Foy airport at L'Ancienne-Lorette is also in my riding, which also has a railway station and a bus terminal. I would say that as far as transportation is concerned, my riding is well provided for. Tertiary services are also adequate, and Sainte-Foy has built sports facilities where some of our gold medal winners have trained.
I know my riding and I know its major issues. As a former municipal councillor in Sainte-Foy, I became acquainted with all the townships. I know the mayors of all four towns in my riding, with their councillors, and also the leaders of organizations and their members. This is a great advantage in serving my constituents to the best of my ability. The residents of Louis-Hebert have a great deal of courage and are able to rise above adversity, and they are also very creative people. For months and even years they have been working on a new economic venture that will benefit the entire Quebec City region. It is incredible to see how well all these organizations, all these people with varying interests are able to work together towards a common goal, and I am thinking, for instance, of the hi-tech industrial park, where high-precision optical and laser instruments will be manufactured.
Mr. Speaker, the riding of Louis-Hebert also has a number of educational institutions including Laval University the oldest francophone university in North-America and also the Sainte-Foy CEGEP, the College Notre-Dame-de-Foy and St. Lawrence College.
Mr. Speaker, you will understand that I am all the more concerned for young people since this year is International Youth Year, which is only fair.
Being a teacher, I can assure you that I am very sensitive to the requests and recommendations made to me by young people. That is why, Mr. Speaker, you will readily understand that I am very pleased about the action taken by the Government to create jobs. As you know, unemployment is a terrible ill facing all young people who enter the labour market and must often resign themselves to live on welfare, because all their efforts and goodwill are often of no avail. All the cases submitted to my constituency office are vivid proof of this fact.
The proposals contained in this Budget, which aim mostly at creating new jobs, can only help these young people to finally join the labour market, and most important, to find permanent employment. In addition, as announced by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) at the First Ministers' Conference in Regina, there is now a Conservative approach to training and employment designed to promote professional training rather than short-term jobs. With such an approach, an increased participation by the private sector and local businesses is essential. That is why, in view of the
May 24, 1985

importance of such an initiative, $900 million have been set aside for these programs this year and an additional amount of $900 million will be allocated in 1986-87. One can only rejoice at such an initiative, which will have a direct impact on these young people looking for a job. I can only approve such a Budget, Mr. Speaker.
In the same connection, the field of research is close to my heart because, obviously, young people will have to live with technological change. High technology is future-oriented and will create a tremendous number of jobs.
Mr. Speaker, the residents of Louis-Hebert are lucky in this regard. Indeed, we have at Laval University, which is very active in the area of research, especially in medicine, optics and laser technology, and elsewhere in the constituency two highly sophisticated scientific complexes, namely, the National Scientific Research Institute, which specializes in water and geological research and also has a second role, that of teaching students at the second and third cycle levels. Moreover, there is the Quebec industrial research centre, which cooperates with industry to develop products as much as possible according to the major directions of the technological approach taken by the Quebec Government.
It was therefore essential that such an important field continue to get federal support, and by refunding 100 per cent of the tax credit earned by small businesses on their first $2 million of qualifying expenditures on research and development each year, the government is making it much easier for new industries which have problems attracting investment capital to expand. Since high technology is a leading sector which will develop even more and become increasingly important in industry, the risk taken by potential investors is most interesting because it is a guarantee of future profitability.
By abolishing the flow-out of the scientific research tax credit to foreign investors, the Canadian Government urges more Canadian investors to take advantage of this measure, and most important, I want to emphasize that it gives them a choice. Everyone is free to invest if and as he chooses.
As I have just pointed out, it must be acknowledged that potential investors are bound to be attracted to this sector because it will continue to expand, thus practically cutting risks down to nothing. It is a safe investment.
Mr. Speaker, this measure will enable the riding of Louis-Hebert to take its rightful place in the technological revolution, ensuring the development of the riding and the creation of jobs related to that sector. Allow me to quote the words of the Right Hon. the Prime Minister when he visited my constituency in 1982:
This region and this riding have everything to become a research and development nerve centre. You have industries, the university, skilled labour, research centres, a social infrastructure and so on. All you need now is the willingness of the federal Government to set targets that reflect the requirements
The Budget-Mrs. Duplessis
of the situation and the talent of our people, and to cooperate with Quebec to turn that into reality.
And today, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to see that the federal Government is willing and anxious to contribute more generously to technological development. I am convinced that the implementation of those measures will enable us to fulfill our aspirations. The Canadian people want to succeed and the residents of my riding share the same ambition. I know them very well, so I have no doubt about that. The harmony which our Government has restored since September 4 between Ottawa and the provinces, particularly the Government of Quebec, augurs well. This dialogue can only benefit all citizens in the constituency of Louis-Hebert, Quebec, and even Canada as a whole.
I can assure the various interest groups of my region that they have my full support in their quest for those objectives. I must emphasize that, through a tax credit, the federal Government will encourage individuals to invest in Quebec's Fonds de solidarite, or in any other similar fund which benefits from provincial tax assistance. Quebec's Fonds de solidarite is a very worthy initiative that came to light after representations were made by the Quebec Federation of Labour to provincial Employment Minister Robert Dean. It is an outstanding example of labour participation in investment projects whose first priority is to help small and medium-sized businesses. It is administered by a 13-member board of directors whose mandate is to invest the funds and make sure that the investments are designed to reach the objectives, namely maintain existing jobs and create new ones.
The tax credit now available in Quebec is one of the best. For instance, someone who would buy 100 shares of $10 today-an investment of $1,000-would in fact have to pay only $187 after eligible tax deductions. In addition to the tax credit already given by the Province of Quebec, the new federal Government tax credit will be a further incentive to make such investments, and the short and long term impact on the economy can only be very positive.
Now, as a woman and a mother, I am very sensitive to the standard of living of women in our society. I am very pleased with the proposals concerning family benefits, which point to this Government's constant concern for the less-privileged in our society.
Many of my constituents were quite apprehensive of a decrease in family allowances. I am proud to reassure them, because these have not been affected. On the contrary, the Government has announced a restructuring of family benefits along the lines of a tax credit. Those changes resulted from suggestions made by a large number of Canadians. Starting in 1986, the Minister of Finance announced that the child tax credit paid to low-income families will be significantly increased to $524 per child as early as 1988, a $140 increase. Moreover, the income level at which the credit begins to phase out will be lowered. Starting in 1987, tax exemption for

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mrs. Duplessis
children will be reduced over a three-year period so that the exemption for children under age 18 will be equal to the level of family allowances. I am very pleased with those measures. They show this Government's concerns for families, the basic structure of our society and the starting point for economic growth. Again this is why I am so pleased with those measures.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 am proud to say that the constituency of Louis-Hebert, the constituency I love so much because of its lively people who are decidedly determined to pull through, is a model of co-operation, and this budget will allow them to fully exercise their initiative and enterpreneurship. These budget measures which are directly aimed at helping small and medium-sized businesses will finally help put people of every age group back to work. They do not privilege any specific group. In that sense, this is a budget that is just and fair for each and every Canadian man and woman. Work is vitally important in our society. By means of this budget, the Canadian Government will enable a very large number of Canadians to recover the dignity they lost with their jobs. Work gives the individual back his or her dignity. This is why it was so essential to deal now with this problem. This Conservative Government, on the other hand, has created 200,000 jobs since September 4, 1984, something which the previous Government could not do in 12 years.
Statistics show also that last month we experienced our largest employment increase in five years, and this is most encouraging. These figures, Mr. Speaker, show how much emphasis my colleagues and myself are laying on the difficult problem of unemployment, and we are willing to do everything that is needed to correct the situation and make sure that economic recovery is effective and producing results as fast as possible. We had to be reasonable and not slash too deeply into the deficit because this would have hurt the less privileged provinces, something which we could not accept. Our sense of justice and fairness would not have it. As any good manager, the Government is aware that it must pay its debt back or at least reduce it, because the astronomical amounts of money needed to pay interests on that debt clearly hinder our economic recovery. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we had no choice, it was an unavoidable obligation.
People of Louis-Hebert, Quebecers, Canadians, have faith in us! This new direction was necessary and urgent on the short and the medium term. I am convinced it will have a very positive impact and will help economic recovery by promoting growth in the private sector. Canadians at last will be able to return to work and regain their dignity, a sine qua non condition for the full development of all individuals. We support small- and medium-size businesses, Mr. Speaker, because we know that their owners who are very good administrators and who feel that a penny saved is worth more that a penny earned will not squander their money. They have repeatedly told us: "Reduce the deficit and pay your debts. We know, because we are involved in trade and commerce, that if
we behaved the way the government has so far, we would have been bankrupt long ago. We do not act irrationally, we tighten our belts and we keep a close watch on our spending." I know that there are employees who accepted salary reductions to keep their jobs when interest rates were so high. They have managed to survive. I know also that there are board chairmen who withdrew their children from private schools, sold their summer cottages, renounced their regular games of golf, lived sparingly and survived those difficult times. Today, we are calling on the Canadian public as a whole to help our country which has run into a financial dead-end and must find a way out. We must revive our economy, create jobs, rationalize government spending, administer with increased efficiency. There will be no increase in the operation and investment budgets of the departments ... I just need a couple of seconds more to conclude, Mr. Speaker. Operation and investment budgets of the departments will no longer be increased to reflect inflation. Each and every one of us must do his or her share, so that our children may live and hope for the dignity which results from the satisfaction of a job well done, raise a family and live as our parents used to before the degrading and decadent Liberal era.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member on her Maiden Speech. It was wonderful and the first of many in the House. I share her tremendous enthusiasm for this Budget. I have been receiving very positive response from my riding of Capilano in British Columbia about the initiatives which the Government is taking.
I think there is an aspect of the Budget that we have not yet discussed to a great degree. One of the major emphasis is, of course, on the development of small business. It is now possible for pension funds and RRSPs to be put into small business. Women are really the engine behind the creation of so many new small businesses. I therefore feel that this Budget is a tremendous boon to the women of the country who have entrepreneurial spirit and want to get involved but have not had the necessary financing. Would the Hon. Member agree that the initiatives we are taking in the Budget will be a great boon to the women of the country in getting their small businesses going and growing and creating the jobs which we all want?
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her kind words and also for her question. The essence of my entire speech was to say that in my opinion the incentives made available to small and medium businesses, especially as far as research and development are concerned, will in the long-term really create jobs. Let me explain that. If small businesses are
May 24, 1985

allowed to invest in research and development and at the end of the year, to recover that money through a tax credit, I think that an increasing number of small industries will explore new avenues and thus create jobs in the long term.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions and comments. Debate. The Hon. Member Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a federal Budget is supposed to do a great many things. First and foremost it is supposed to be about ordinary, everyday people. It should assure them that their Government is listening to them, cares for them, and is committed to ensuring equal opportunity for careers, education, recreation and retirement. A Budget should be about people and their lives, but this Budget is about none of those things. It gives none of those assurances. It is cold and insensitive. It is a statement which fails to understand the urgent needs of Canadian women, of youth, and of the elderly. It has taken this cynical, unfeeling Budget to flush the Conservative Government out on where it stands on issues that really matter to the general population, to Monsieur, Madame, tout le monde. The sound of cold hard cash rings through this Budget ripping holes in our social safety net, but the voices of ordinary Canadian men and women have not been heard.
Canadians had great expectations and hopes for this Budget. The Government consulted and consulted, but reality indicates that this much-touted consultation process has been an utter flop. We waited for more than eight months to see which lobby would win the day. It is not very difficult to discern. The big business boys, the multinationals, the oil companies and the defence industry are the winners. The Government listened to them. I can only hope that the women, the youth, and the labour leaders invited to be consulted at the national economic conference were at least given a cup of coffee and a doughnut, because that is about all they got out of this Budget.
Harry Truman once said, "When you can't convince them, confuse them". The Tories have tried that often enough. Now the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has gone one better. When you can't confuse, consult.
A federal Budget is also supposed to answer questions and remove uncertainty. This one has done exactly the reverse. Canadians now have more questions than ever before about the Government's secret agenda for social programs and social policy. There are questions about what is going to happen with the maternity benefits program and the unemployment insurance scheme. There is more uncertainty than ever before about how the Government intends to replace the cuts in job creation and training programs. These cuts severely hurt the efforts of youth to find meaningful, lasting work. The lack of detail on the Government's proposed $900 million labour strategy is absolutely shocking and frustrating. You had better check your Budget because I believe that $900 million is not new money. It is renewed from last year.
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
I listened to the Budget speech yesterday with great care and a good deal of hope. I listened on behalf of women in the workplace, women working in the home, women struggling to make ends meet for their families, women retired on fixed incomes, and women living below the poverty line. I listened on behalf of young people who were promised so much in the last election but have seen so little. I was listening and hoping. However, today I share the bitter disappointment of these women and young people in the reality of this barren Budget.
Before touching on areas on areas of specific concern to women and youth I would like to say a few words about the tone and underlying message of this Budget. Through this tone we see clearly how the Government has ignored the forces of ordinary men and women. In the fourth paragraph on the first page the Minister said:
My Budget calls for Canadians, not government, to choose what is best for Canada. And it challenges Canadians by rewarding success, not subsidizing effort.
I thought that sheer effort and pride in one's work used to be the motto for this society. Apparently now only successful financial effort is of worth. I think the ordinary folk of society will not be very pleased with that.
Further down I see a description of how the discussion process took place. Page 17 contains that marvellous part of the Budget about de-indexing. It reads:
The purpose of indexation has been to protect Canadians from the effects of rising prices. But it has become increasingly clear that Canadians must also find a way to protect themselves against rising deficits and the soaring national debt.
I would like to have that told to single-parent families, to single mothers, the elderly and the poor. How are they going to protect themselves against this rising deficit and the soaring national debt? I am sure they got a tremendous sense of satisfaction from that remark. When you tell people that it is about time they started to pull their own weight to protect themselves, I think it is a bit unfair. This is what I mean when I say that the Budget is cold, insensitive and that it lacks a human face and a human heart.
I could go on. There are so many matters of affront in the tone and the text of the Budget that I am almost ashamed that this is our Government speaking out. Let us look at what the Government says about particular benefits to women, something I will deal with later. As a woman reading what the Government appears to think about me, I wonder about this Government's supposed interest in the other sex.
I want to turn to several points in the Government's Budget that are deeply disturbing to me and I believe to millions of Canadian women and young people.
Canadians expected training for women and youth to be a top priority in this Budget. How often did we hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) chant "jobs, jobs, jobs"? What did the Minister of Finance say? From where did he get his guidance? He said absolutely nothing about youth. The guidance he got was from the Nielsen Task Force. It was to address all those concerns particularly relating to youth and

May 24, 1985
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
women, areas of major unemployment. The Task Force was to look at and determine the kinds of programs women and youth should have. 1 would suggest that Members on the other side of this House take a look at the list of people used in all this wonderful consultative process and notice the absence of the distaff side. There was an absence of women and young people on the committees used by the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen). This makes me very sad for the future of training. What about the cutting that will take place?
We have had Budget cuts in general and critical skills training of $78 million. Young people will have to wait until the fall to hear of any replacement programs. High-tech job training is precisely what young men and women need. Upgrading of skills is essential for women and for youth to secure better-paying jobs. Nearly 500,000 young people are out of work. Yet this Government chooses to cut funds for highly skilled job training. Are we to return to the days when we trained young women to be hairdressers?
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Budget's job creation efforts rely totally on the private sector, the same folks who brought us the situation in which women are blocked from promotion, still earn less than men for work of equal value, and still discriminate against women. This is a hope and a prayer job creation strategy and it is doomed to condemn women to job ghettos.
The Government has also created undue uncertainty over the status of the unemployment insurance scheme. Of particular concern to women is the future of maternity benefits. Maternity benefits are a right not a social benefit or a privilege. They are an important bridge for women who wish to continue to work after childbirth. Since 70 per cent of the recipients do return to the job market, I think they have indicated their attachment to the program. It is obvious this program is an integral part of their economic independence. We will be monitoring the Government's plans in this area very carefully. Canada already ranks near the very bottom among industrialized nations when it comes to ensuring paid parental leave. Now is not the time to chip away at this further.
Speaking of chipping away, let it not go by unnoticed that the great majority of federal civil service jobs cut by this Budget will be or are held by women. More than 40 per cent of federal employees are women, many in the lower paid positions which will be most vulnerable to cuts.
Let me speak about pensions. Pensions are a fundamental building block for women as they seek economic independence and autonomy. The Government's Budget has done very little to improve pension opportunities for women. Contrary to election promises, there are no provisions for homemakers in the proposals. The Government's plan to improve vesting rights in employer-sponsored pension plans is as far as it goes. It will in the end benefit few women. Only one third of Canadian women in the labour force are enrolled in private pension plans, because most women work for small companies that have no such employer-sponsored plan, or they are parttime workers with no access to pensions. Do not forget that 70
per cent of all part-time workers in Canada are women, and not necessarily by choice.
The Minister of Finance has also backed away from any Canada Pension Plan improvements. He has bowed to business pressure and backed away from any federal leadership role in mandating a minimum degree of inflation protection for private pension plans, a key part of any reform package. A comfortable pension at age 65 can be eroded by inflation by age 75 without some form of protection. Inflation protection is not a frill but an essential component.
Canadians can add the improvement of pension reform to the growing list of empty campaign promises of this Government.
Let me come to housing now, Mr. Speaker. And what about child care and child benefits? What about federal transfers to the provinces? What about the entire area of youth?

I think, with all respect that the Opposition Parties, both of them, if they would look at their numbers, have as much a duty to attend the Chamber as we do.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Proportionately we have more than you. It is your Budget, your quorum.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a silent crisis ongoing in our country that this Government does not seem to be aware of. I am speaking of housing, aging buildings, low vacancy rates in almost every major city and hald a million Canadians unable to afford decent housing. The victims in this crisis are too often women, single mothers and elderly women on low incomes. Yet, this Government has cut the Budget for CMHC and this has far-reaching impact.

One Canadian woman out of ten is battered. Last year, the Canadian Mortgage and Housing Corporation gave funds to start only 11 shelters with a total of 129 beds. There are presently in Canada only 190 shelters and three projects for the next stage, Mr. Speaker, you are well aware of the Badgley and Fraser reports which were tabled and which emphasize the need for these shelters. More than 500,000 Canadian women
May 24, 1985

are victims of family violence. The Mulroney budget concluded that $26 million from the CMHC suited their needs perfectly.

Let me speak about federal transfers to the provinces, Mr. Speaker. There is another important part of the Budget that will have far-reaching impacts for women and youth in Canada. I am referring to the Government's intention to deindex federal transfers to the provinces and further to reduce such transfers by $2 billion by the end of the decade. So much for the Prime Minister's co-operative federalism.
The real danger is that this federal action will put increasing pressure on the provinces to take a hard look at how they are going to finance such programs as transition homes for battered women, welfare payments, medicare and university tuition. These are the kinds of hidden and sneaky cuts that this Budget is really all about. They are the kinds of cuts which show the true priorities of the Tories.
I could deal with child care and child benefits. I could tell you that I feel terrible that there was nothing about daycare in
The Budget-Mrs. Finestone
the Budget. Last and most important is our youth. This cutting of job training and the abandonment of direct job-creation efforts have bitterly disappointed the youth of Canada. The Canadian Federation of Students called me-
